Ladies and gentlemen, I am about to start the meeting. Please take your seat. The last time and then we start. The fifth plenary meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. Please take your seat. Before proceeding to the general debate, the Assembly will hear an introduction by the Secretary-General of his annual report on the work of the Organization, under agenda item 113, in accordance with resolution 51/241 of 31 July 1997. I now give the floor. Before I give the floor to Secretary General, this is my final call. Please be seated. I now give the floor to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, His Excellency Antonio Guterres.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, The fault lines in our world are widening. Cracks have become canyons. Over the last day, over the last decade, wars erupted with devastating consequences and dragged on with despicable cruelty. Civilians were targeted, human rights trampled, hunger weaponized, humanitarians killed, international law cast aside, and geopolitical divides have deepened and inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. And the climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality, and artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it. These are not separate crises. They are chapters of the same story, the story of power. Who has it? Who is denied? How it is used and how it is changing. Excellencies, Power is being reshaped in three fundamental ways. First, among states, new centers of economic, political, and technological influence have emerged. Second, we are witnessing an extraordinary transfer of power away from governments to handful of private corporations and individuals. Their reach now extends across politics, economies, information flows, technological development, and the civic space on which societies depend. And third, humans are increasingly handing power to machines, with artificial agents going rogue and little autonomous weapons going from science fiction to military reality. Yet, our institutions and systems of governance continue to reflect the power realities and interests of a largely bygone era. That is the defining challenge before us. At the very moment when humanity faces an unprecedented convergence of threats, our mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain. Excellencies, we are clearly moving towards a multipolar world, and that movement is irreversible. But there are different ways that multipolarity can take shape. One possibility is a world of fragmentation and transactionalism, a world of rising tensions and deepening mistrust, of fractured markets and weakened institutions, of shrinking cooperation and zero-sum calculations. And in many respects, that is the trajectory we are on today. But there is another path. a path towards networked multipolarity, a world built on interdependence and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social, and technological connections, a world in which multiple centers of influence coexist with a common framework of international law and shared rules. And such a world can help us avoid hegemonic tendencies and also what I have called the great fracture, the division of the world into two rival blocks with separate economic, technological, and security systems. We must avoid them. A networked world recognizes that no power can solve today's challenges alone. Of course, competition will remain a permanent feature of international relations. But competition does not have to mean confrontation. Healthy competition can drive innovation, strengthen resilience, and expand opportunity. But only when it operates within the frameworks that preserve stability and enable cooperation where cooperation is indispensable. Building a networked future begins with the recognition, especially by superpowers, that their power isn't so super, that their power has limits. And the events of recent years have made that unmistakably clear. Military power alone cannot secure peace. Economic power alone cannot command stability. And technological power alone cannot guarantee security. A networked multipolar world can create the conditions for more balanced and representative global problem solving. But it requires a multilateral system centered in the UN that is balanced and representative, strong, effective institutions that reflect the realities and progressively changing relative weight of countries and economies in today's world, not the power arrangements of 80 years ago. Fortunately, we are not starting from scratch. We already have a binding foundation, the Charter of the United Nations, and the principles that give it life. The primacy of international law, upholding human dignity, and the pursuit of justice in all its dimensions. These are the backbone for the effective, legitimate, and responsible exercise of power in the 21st century. Excellencies, it comes down to this. Will we act to ensure that power is governed by law or by force, by cooperation or coercion, by responsibility to young people and future generations, or indifference to their fate? Because the defining challenges of our age are not separate from the question of power, they are expressions of it. And they will determine whether we drift deeper into division and instability or move toward cooperation, justice, and collective security. Looking ahead, our future will be shaped by how we address four great tests of power: the power over war and peace; The power that concentrates wealth and drives inequality. The power fueling climate chaos and war on nature. And the power unleashed by artificial intelligence. Excellencies, the first great power test in the 21st century is peace and security. Peace is far more than the absence of conflict. It is the presence of restraint of power by law. It is the recognition, as enshrined in the UN Charter, that force cannot be the final arbiter of whose lives, rights and future matter. Today, that principle is under profound strain. Across the Middle East, conflicts are escalating. So-called ceasefires have amounted to little more than lesser fires, with civilians continuing to pay the price. Enough is enough. I appeal to the leaders in this chamber to maximize this high-level week for de-escalation and dialogue. And together, let's send a clear message from this hall: the fighting must stop, humanitarian aid must flow, and navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in accordance with international law. Amid the turmoil engulfing the region, we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territory. It is nearly three years since the abhorrent terror attacks by Hamas on 7 October. But what followed was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza with a scale of killing and destruction and like anything I've witnessed in my years as Secretary-General. The International Court of Justice has issued legally binding provisional measures in the case entitled, and I quote, "Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip," end of quote. In advisory opinion last year, The court was clear that United Nations need to be allowed to perform our mandates in Gaza and for our staff and humanitarian personnel to be protected. All parties must comply with international law and the court's orders. Meanwhile, violence, displacement, and settlement expansion by Israel in the occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the specter of ethnic cleansing. We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes. In Ukraine, Russia's full-scale invasion has subjected a sovereign country to a brutal war in blatant violation of the Charter. Civilians continue to be killed far from the front lines. mainly in Ukraine, but also more recently in parts of Russia. Homes, energy and water systems and transport have come under repeated attack, threatening food and energy supply chains globally. In Sudan, a war for raw power fed by outside actors has become a war on civilians. Millions displaced, anger spreading, drone striking hospitals and homes, sexual violence and ethnically driven attacks escalating, and the country being torn apart as the world looks away. And in Myanmar, another crisis at risk of slipping from global attention, with escalating violence, mass displacement, and expanding transnational crime. Excellencies, These and so many other conflicts show what happens when power gets out of control, force outpaces diplomacy, military budgets soar, and accountability goes out the window. The test before us is whether power will be exercised with the law or beyond it. And we must pass that test. We must defend the Charter without double standards, protect civilians without exception, ensure humanitarian access without obstruction, shield humanitarian personnel without fail, advance nuclear nonproliferation and disarmament without delay, and demand accountability without fear or favor. And we must also reform the Security Council so that it reflects today's world with the legitimacy and effectiveness that today's challenges demand. The Security Council was designed in the aftermath of World War II, but the world has fundamentally changed since then, a change that is far from reflected in the Security Council. The most stunning example is Africa. When the UN was founded, most of Africa was still under colonial rule. Today, Africa still has no permanent representation on the Council. A 21st century Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible. This must change.

Excellencies, the second test of power is inequality. Inequality is often framed as an economic problem, but it is a power problem. Power over opportunity and who has it, access to resources, voice. Never has humanity possessed so much wealth, knowledge and technological capability, yet for billions of human beings, progress remains out of reach. They see prosperity around them. but not for themselves in their own lives. They are told that globalization expands horizons, but they only experience exclusion. They are promised that technology will unlock new possibilities, yet many fear it will take away their livelihoods. Meanwhile, Billions of people still live today without the essentials embedded in the sustainable development goals that should be guaranteed for everyone. Food, clean water, education, decent work, healthcare, dignity, excellences. No country should be denied a sustainable future because it is on the wrong side of a deeply unequal financial system. And yet, so many throughout the developing world are being crushed by unsustainable debt, battered by disasters they did little to cause, and locked out of affordable finance. This is why we have created political spaces to bring forward a reform of the international financial architecture. This is not a technical debate. It is a question of representation, of fairness, and of sharing of power. For debt relief that is timely, effective, and just. For multilateral development banks that are bigger, bolder, and better equipped to provide affordable, long-term finance at scale. and massively leverage private finance for special drawing rights to benefit countries that need the most.

No discussion of inequality can ignore its most universal form, the inequality between women and men. Everywhere, Women and girls continue to face discrimination, violence, exclusion, and abuse. Around the world, their rights are being rolled back, their voices silenced, their bodies turned into battlegrounds, and their freedoms treated as bargaining chips. This is an outrage and a profound waste for humanity. Peace is more durable when women are at the table. Economies are more dynamic when women have equal opportunity. Societies are more resilient when girls can learn, lead, and live free from fear. And institutions are more effective when power is shared equally. Over the last decade, we achieved an enormous milestone. I am proud to report to you today that the United Nations achieved gender parity for the first time in history across all senior leadership, all headquarters, and all professional staff. It happened because we removed barriers, we challenged assumptions, and refused to accept that power must look as it always was. At every step, we have never compromised on quality and competence. Equality is not a dream, it is a decision. If the United Nations can change, so can governments, so can parliaments, so can businesses, so can peace processes, and so can this General Assembly. Excellencies, the third great power test is the climate crisis. In many ways, it's the most profound intergenerational power imbalance of all. one generation consuming the future of the next, one group profiting while those least responsible suffer first and worst. Three years ago in the mountains of Nepal, I sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt, warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in. Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers, but as tragic events have shown, Impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder, and spreading further than many anticipated. Now we face a near certain breach of the 1.5 degree limit with a super-sized El Nino speeding straight for humanity. The dangers are real, but so is the hope. The last decade has fueled one of the most promising shifts in power of our time, the rise of clean energy. The sun belongs to no one. The wind cannot be embargoed. Innovation can come from everywhere. And this is a profound rebalancing of power relations. Renewables are now the cheapest source of new electricity in most of the world, and the most viable path to energy security, independence, and sustainable growth. Excellencies, a future beyond fossil fuels is in sight. The question is how. Will it be a just and orderly transition built on international cooperation, or chaotic and costly, leaving people and countries behind? Today, I call on every government to adopt a national plan to transition away from fossil fuels aligned with 1.5 degrees, with clear timelines and protection for affected workers and communities. We know that fossil fuel interests won't step aside on their own. For decades, Big Oil has treated the atmosphere as an open sewer and cashed in on the consequences. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits. Compare that with just $34 billion in international public adaptation finance for developing countries in the latest year reported. Meanwhile, everyday people are paying more for energy, food, and insurance. And we have seen this kind of abuse of power before. When the harms of big tobacco became undeniable, governments acted. And the climate crisis demands the same determination. Those who polluted the most and profited the most must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay. And to the leaders, cities, civil society and citizens working to hold them accountable, I say you are on the right side of history. Keep going and governments must keep going on all fronts to end deforestation. invest in grids and storage, cut methane emissions. But these actions are not enough. We need climate justice with a focus on adaptation and finance. Developed countries must respect their commitments. They must triple adaptation finance and make the loss and damage fund work at scale. The present funds available in the loss and damage fund are ridiculously small. We must also ensure that the mining of critical minerals does not dig deeper into the inequalities of the past. Producing countries and affected communities must retain a far greater share of the value created from their resources. No more plundering. No more exploitation. Excellencies, the first power test is technology and above all, artificial intelligence. For centuries, power came from territory, then industry, then finance. Today, power increasingly comes from data, computing capacity, and algorithms. And this new power is highly concentrated, and it's advancing at extraordinary speed, and racing ahead of our ability to understand its full consequences. In 2017, AI was barely on the world's radar. Yet in my first address to the opening of the General Assembly, I warned, and I quote, "Artificial intelligence is a game changer that can boost development and transform lives in spectacular fashion, but it may also have a dramatic impact on labor markets and indeed on global security and the very fabric of societies." End of quote. Here we are almost a decade later. And it is indeed a game changer with enormous promise to advance medicine, accelerate scientific discovery, expand opportunity and improve lives. But make no mistake, the danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability, capability without oversight, decision making without transparency, and that danger can be minimized. The very developers building these systems are now pulling the alarm. Excellencies, the first duty of governments is to protect their people. Governments must assume their responsibilities. And governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust, and cooperation, not despite geopolitical rivalry, but precisely because of it. At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks. They built mechanisms to reduce misunderstanding, manage escalation, and prevent catastrophe. At that time, it was the nuclear armament. Today, artificial intelligence demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency. Those countries leading this technological revolution must share information on emerging safety risks, cooperate on testing and evaluation, and work towards common safeguards that protect us all. But because this affects us all, global coordination is indispensable. And there is only one place where every country has a voice in shaping our common future. And that place is the United Nations. Through the Global Digital Compact, you agreed for the first time on universal principles for AI governance. Through the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, we created a platform for governments, scientists, industry, leaders, and civil society to work together. Through the independent international scientific panel on AI, we have brought together global expertise to ensure that policy is guided by evidence. Just yesterday, the AI scientific panel released a thematic brief on AI safety and risks from loss of human control. Building on these efforts, we must take the next steps. First, to advance the conditions for the responsible pacing of AI and the additional safeguards needed to address risks. Second, to work towards a multilateral AI risk management framework supported by credible and independent oversight. In all our efforts, we must ensure no country is left behind. Artificial intelligence must be shaped by humanity, with humanity, and for all humanity. And as we confront the challenges ahead, Let us not retreat from two fundamental principles. Let's say with one voice, children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems. And let us resolve that life and death decisions must never be surrendered to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future.

Excellences, peace and security, inequality, climate, artificial intelligence. These are the four great power tests of the future. They will define the future and they're interlinked. War deepens inequality, destroys development and accelerates hunger. Inequality determines who has the means to face climate change and other shocks and who is left exposed to the dangers. The climate crisis fuels instability and displacement. Artificial intelligence could help solve all these challenges, or it could make them worse.

Across all four tests, the decisive issue is power. Power over force, money, energy, technology, rules, and the future. And that is why the UN Charter and the work of the United Nations matter more than ever. The United Nations exists because power requires rules, and humanity needs a place where power answers to principle. And the Charter leaves no room for selective reading. The Charter created an organization rooted in three pillars: peace, development, and human rights. And these are not competing agendas. They are one reality. There is no peace without development, no development without peace, and no peace and development without human rights. To pretend that peace can be separated from dignity, opportunity, and rights is an unacceptable illusion. But defending these truths does not mean defending the status quo. The Pact for the Future and UN8 initiatives always respected the principle of equality of the three pillars of the United Nations, and about making the UN more responsive, more effective, more coherent, more transparent, more focused on results, more disciplined on resources, and more present where people need us. The world does not need a weaker United Nations. It needs a UN strong enough to face the world as it is and determined enough to build the world as it should be. Excellencies, after 10 years, I hold one conviction even more strongly than when I have arrived. The greatest power is not the power to dominate. It is the power to build a future that works for everyone. Our shared future will be forged by whether humanity can govern power wisely, by upholding the law before impunity becomes normalized, by ending wars before they consume generations, by tackling inequality before society is fractured, by accelerating climate action before tipping points are crossed, and by governing artificial intelligence before it governs us. This is the challenge before this General Assembly, the United Nations, and humanity itself. Ecologies. In the face of global catastrophe more than eight years ago, the United Nations was created as an act of defiance, the defiance of people who refuse to surrender the future to fear, the defiance against the self-defeating notion that might makes right, the defiance of countries that now our futures are bound together the defiance of hope. I will carry that spirit of resolve and determination through each of the 100 days I have left in office. But commitment to values and principles of the United Nations does not begin with a mandate, and it does not end with one. They are greater than an office, and they endure beyond any life. So on January 1, when I am no longer Secretary-General, Be sure of this, wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible, that human dignity is universal, that the power of law must prevail over the law of power, and that our common future is worth fighting for. I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter, and I will never ever give up. Thank you.

I thank you, Mr. Secretary-General. The Assembly will now turn to agenda item 8, entitled General Debate. I will now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, Mr. Secretary General, former Presidents of the General Assembly, ladies and gentlemen, 40 years ago, I stood in this very hall as a newly minted member of the cabinet of the 41st President of the General Assembly, Mr. Humayun Rashid Chaudhry. At that time, he said, and I quote, In recent years, there appears to have been a crisis of confidence in the United Nations itself. There is a general feeling that the United Nations today needs revitalizing in a number of aspects in order to bring it into line with the priorities of a changing world. That was 40 years ago. Questions about multilateralism and the effectiveness of the United Nations, therefore, are not new. They have been part of this place since the first stone was laid. Yet, through it all, the United Nations has persevered, not because it is perfect, but because it is irreplaceable, and because the alternative is simply unfathomable. The world of 1945 was in peril. The Second World War, the colossal devastation wrought by it, and the Holocaust left humanity bankrupt, morally and fiscally. Something had to change, and this place was that change. It ushered in a long era of diplomacy, which continues, Member States coming together to work through their problems because they knew that the alternative, guns blazing and bombs dropping, simply was not an option. Perhaps the clearest evidence of its achievements is here in this very hall. In 1945, 50 nations participated in the San Francisco Conference. Today, eight decades later, the organization has 193 member states. The UN has brought together humanity under one roof. This is unprecedented in human history. The core promise of this institution is, has, was, and remains to prevent the unimaginable, a third world war. The fact that we have avoided such calamity is among the greatest achievements this institution could ever deliver. But survival alone cannot be our sole measure of success. Outside these walls, people are not asking whether the United Nations still exists. They are asking whether it works. Yes, there have been wars and conflicts that we could not prevent and issues we could not resolve. The Palestinian issue continues unresolved for decades, as the Secretary-General just alluded to.

Wars and conflict and their aftermath are ravaging Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar, and the Middle East. But even as those wars raged, the United Nations stayed and served. I have seen it up close in my own country, Bangladesh, where the United Nations country team in Cox's Bazar is striving to do more with less to support Rohingya refugees in the camps who are yearning to return back to Myanmar. Just recently, a representative from a war-torn nation said to me, "Your peacekeepers from Bangladesh were not just blue helmets. They built roads and communities. They fed children. They helped rebuild societies and put us on the road to proper governance." In Iraq, the United Nations system helped nearly 5 million people return home. It rehabilitated hundreds of schools, electricity stations, and water treatment plants. And right now, in Haiti, the entire United Nations family is delivering amid immense security and governance challenges. These stories rarely make headlines, but we should never lose sight of what it is that is working. At the same time, let us not turn a blind eye to where we have fallen short, particularly in a world where challenges seem to multiply by the day. And newer challenges appear every day. The war in Gaza has left over 70,000 people dead, including thousands of children. Humanitarian support has been a fraction of what is needed. The ongoing wars across the Middle East and Europe have consequences far beyond the front lines. and the heartbreaking natural disaster in Nepal and China was not just an isolated event, but yet another horrible climax to our collectively insufficient response to climate change. The circumstances and the politics of this crisis differ, but our commitment under the United Nations Charter do not. The principles of multilateralism, International law, international humanitarian law, the protection of civilians and humanitarian access cannot be applied selectively, not if we want the world to trust us. It is precisely at such times that we must honestly confront our setbacks, however profound, not with blame, cynicism or blind hope, but with action, sober reflection, clear-eyed realism and pragmatism. This is how we chart these turbulent waters. And this is what we need to rebuild trust in this institution, the central focus of this session and my statement. So how do we build back trust? Trust is not given. It is earned. And we earn trust, I believe, in three ways. First, by being unapologetically realistic about where we are falling behind. Second, by taking a foundational look at the reforms of the United Nations to deliver better. And third, by making our work inclusive and engaging all relevant stakeholders from all parts of our society. Let me elaborate. On my first point, we must be frank about where the challenges lie and what needs to be fixed, even when the necessary changes may prove painful. consider peace and security one of the pillars of the organization. Under the UN Charter, the Security Council bears primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Yet, when the Council is unable to act, member states turn to the General Assembly. We saw this as early as 1950 with the Uniting for Peace resolution, and we have seen it more recently through the Assembly's veto initiative. These two principal organs of our organization are complementary, not competing. The Charter provides for an appropriate balance between them. Both chambers must do their respective part. To be fair, the Security Council, when it acts, proves its strength and effectiveness. It helped liberate Kuwait, ended civil war in El Salvador, supported Namibia's independence, led rebuilding of Colombia, Cambodia and stabilized conflict-affected countries through peacekeeping. Yet, when the Council is unable to act on important matters, the effectiveness of our Organization as a whole is called into question. In 1945, humanity placed its trust in the Council in good faith, giving it the extraordinary responsibility of maintaining international peace and security. The Council accepted that responsibility and entered into a compact. It must now hold up its end of the bargain. This is what the people of the world expect. And in their eyes, when the Security Council works, the United Nations works. The promise of 1945 still binds us today. I call on the Security Council and all of its members to step up, to lead as we need it to lead, and to act when we need it to act. Linked to this is the question of Security Council reform. I will support General Assembly-led intergovernmental negotiations. in its work to make the Council more representative, transparent and reflective of the geopolitical realities of our time. Ensuring fair representation for underrepresented regions must remain a priority. As the Secretary-General has said, nowhere is this more important right now than in Africa. After eight decades, the largest region by number of Member States and a key focus of UN peacekeeping, remains underrepresented on the Security Council. Africa needs to be at the table, not on the menu. Africa cannot be asked to wait indefinitely for the rightful place on the Council. Ending Africa's underrepresentation now is a question of fairness, justice, and ultimately the credibility of this organization. Turning to the development pillar, and particularly the Sustainable Development Goals, we are right to focus on the challenges. Last year, OECD donors spent about $175 billion on development assistance, a whopping 23% drop year on year. And yet, military expenditures approached $3 trillion, capping 11 straight years of growth. All the while, progress on the SDGs stalled at just over a third of targets, And developing countries are now paying the price for supply chain disruptions they did not cause and cannot cure. The contrast could not be more stark. We must better prioritize on how we spend our resources by augmenting development assistance, addressing debt burdens, reforming the international financial architecture, fulfilling our CVIA and Paris commitments. and implementing the programs of actions for least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing states as well as African Union's Agenda 2063. Because where we have done so, the results are clear. Over the past decade, nearly 1 billion people have gained access to safely managed drinking water. Electricity now reaches 92% of world's population, very close to universality. And internet access has risen from 40% to 74%. Behind these numbers are healthier children, more resilient communities, greater opportunities for women and girls, and renewed hope. These gains show that accelerating the SDGs is possible when developing countries and the development partners work in concert and this is indeed a shared responsibility. Developing countries must also intensify their own efforts through domestic resource mobilization and plug any leakage or corruption, including capital flight, a plague that until recently undermined development in my own country under a repressive and authoritarian regime. Turning to human rights, we should acknowledge that these are central to the other two pillars. They can promote peace. There cannot be peace without rights and advanced sustainable development. And we recognize one of the most urgent assaults on human dignity today, hate speech that incites violence. It is a growing threat to regional and global peace, and it is on the rise. Hateful narratives are spreading like wildfire across borders and into homes at unprecedented speed and scale. They target women and girls, minorities, migrants, refugees and persons with disabilities, often for political gain. New and emerging technologies are used to amplify lies, manipulate public debate, spread hatred, and give incitement to violence faster and farther than ever before. We must choose dialogue and tolerance and foster a culture in which human rights are respected, not only in law, but in our daily interactions. And we must stop cherry-picking of those rights that fit our respective cultures or politics of the day. Whether it is Islamophobia, anti-Semitism, homophobia, misogyny, it's all the same. Hatred repackaged and relabeled. Let us use the tools of our age, not to deepen fear, but to widen understanding and advance human dignity for everyone, everywhere. My second point, making the United Nations fit for the future, which requires a more foundational approach to reform. The UN80 initiative is a constructive start. Thank you, Mr. Secretary-General, for this. But it is only a start. Moving positions on a budget sheet may deliver savings. Merging or renaming bodies may reduce duplication. Streamlining structures may improve efficiency. These steps are important and often essential for good housekeeping, but they are not enough. We need to dig deeper to address the problems beneath the superstructure because the United Nations reform challenges are chronic and fundamental. On 24 November 1949, barely four years after the founding of the United Nations, this Assembly adopted resolution 310 entitled "Problems of proliferation and overlapping of programs of the United Nations and of the specialized agencies. It urged member states, and I quote, "to refrain from initiating new projects other than those which are urgently required and which can be effectively carried out." Yet we have not paid sufficient attention to our own decision. We have since created thousands of mandates, of which 4,000 are still active, irrespective of whether they were required or could be effectively carried out. We cannot continue treating a chronic ailment with temporary painkillers when what we need is a deeper diagnosis and a more profound plan for transformation, even if that plan proves painful. And here I must be equally candid. This will happen only if Member States take charge. Time and again, we say that United Nations reforms must be member-led, which looks like a tacit admission that they are not. Too often, we Member States fail to take the wheel. Passive ownership is not enough. If we do not claim proactive ownership of this place, we cannot expect it to self-heal. So let us engage, let us take charge, fix our own house, respect sovereignty of Member States, and together deliver the transformation we need. As we decide what must change, we must also recognize what already works. Again and again, Member States tell us that the United Nations works well at the country level, emergency situations, and in keeping and building peace. We should build on that success. We should strengthen the United Nations work in these areas and draw increasingly on local capacity, including qualified national institutions and individuals. including women and young people. We should ensure that all activities at the country level from development, support to peacekeeping and are properly integrated and produce the highest synergy. We should ensure avoidance of turf battles among different parts of the UN and exercise care to select the leaders at the country level that are fit to lead. We want to have full value for money. Let's remember, The organization's financial viability remains a chronic concern. We must ensure that it receives sufficient resources on a sustained basis and that all countries paid their dues on time and without conditions. We should also recognize that dues to the United Nations come from hard-working places all around the world. Every penny must therefore be properly accounted for. Every penny must be invested to achieve impact on the ground for the people we serve. The role of the Member States, supported by the Secretariat, is essential to delivering our work, but not sufficient. This brings me to my third point, building a more open and inclusive United Nations. We know that the United Nations of today and the world it serves are profoundly different from those of 1945. Nowhere is the pace of change more evident today than in artificial intelligence. AI can be a powerful accelerator of human progress. Therefore, we must not close the door to innovation. At the same time, we must address AI's potential harms, including job losses and widening of the digital divide. We cannot also rule out the possibility that AI, particularly artificial general intelligence or AGI, could affect the very human survival. That demands prudent and reliable guardrails based on scientific evidence to safeguard the global public interest while allowing innovation to go forward. Governments must remain at the heart of this endeavor. But governments do not have a monopoly on expertise, capital, technology, innovation, or influence. Much of that experience and capacity already lies with businesses, innovators, civil society, and others. We need to keep the doors of United Nations unlocked to those developing and using AI. Not someday, now. And we are falling further as we are falling further behind each day. AI differs from earlier proliferation challenges in one critical respect. It is already embedded in nearly every facet of our lives, in our water systems, electricity grids, economies, and militaries. We cannot allow an arms race for control of AI to carry us over the precipice. There is clear precedent for the United Nations engagement with world-changing developments. We did so on nuclear nonproliferation. through the Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer and with the United Nations Declaration on Human Cloning in 2005. We need experts, innovators, industry leaders, scientists, civil society and academia, all working together with member states on these issues of our times. We regard the elevation of our relations with ASEAN to the level of dialogue partnership as a concrete outcome of this approach. Likewise, we are developing our relations with the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean on the basis of mutual respect, partnership and a win-win approach. Distinguished members, We all derive our livelihood and the source of our life from nature. But our world stands on the threshold of serious environmental and climate-related threats. Air, water and soil, and also many living species, are being affected by climate change. While developing countries and the Pacific region are experiencing the climate crisis to their very core, they unfortunately face serious difficulties in accessing the funding they need. This November, we'll host the COP31 summit in Antalya province of Turkey. At the summit, will ensure that climate justice is given particular prominence. With the partnership we have developed with Australia, we aim to make COP31 an implementation COP, where financial commitments are fulfilled, technology transfer is accelerated, and promises are actually translated into concrete steps. So, COP31 will be made a point of uniting us all. And taking this opportunity, I invite you to the COP31 Leaders Summit. In 2017, my wife, Mrs. Emine Erdogan, initiated the Zero Waste Movement with the slogan, "The world is our common home." And this initiative has now evolved into a global campaign to raise awareness. It is a fact that there are for sure many ways to tackle the climate crisis. The zero waste movement is the strongest bridge where all these paths meet. I believe that with your support, this bridge will become even stronger. I would also like to draw your attention to the following fact. Another threat as serious as climate change is the spread of a culture of waste fueled by an incredible desire for consumption. Every year, 5.8 trillion plates or servings of food end up in the garbage bin worldwide, meaning that more than 2 billion tons of food are being wasted. We cannot speak of justice in a world where tons of food are thrown into the garbage on one side, while hundreds of millions of people collect food from garbage containers on the other. As Turkey, we are ready to make every possible contribution, both to preventing waste and to ensuring global food security. So with this understanding in mind, we have nominated Dr. Mehmet Mehdi Eker for the position of Director General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN. I'm confident that you will not withhold your support for our candidate. Now, it is also worth noting the following. As our world changes fast, humanity has concurrently began to face new social threats. Islamophobia, which is spreading like a plague in the West, is at the forefront of these issues. It is long overdue now to establish a common international legal framework for AI. It is crucial to accelerate the work which is already being carried out to draft and bring into force the UN International Convention on Artificial Intelligence. Distinguished delegates, the Realities I've spoken of here today with an open heart will for sure upset some people, will for sure disrupt their comfort and unmask their lies. I also know well that they will resort to all kinds of perception management operations in an attempt to silence our voice. A late poet said the following quote, They think that if we remain silent, the issue will disappear. But even if we remain silent, history will not. Even if history remains silent, the truth will not. They believe that if they get rid of us, the problem will be solved. Yet, even if they get rid of us, they will not be able to escape the pangs of their own conscience. Even if they escape the pangs of their conscience, they will not be able to escape the pangs of history. Even if they escape the pangs of history, they will not be able to escape the punishment of God." Unquote. as Tayyip Erdogan, as the president of a great nation guided by its conscience, its history and its compassion. God willing, for as long as God grants me life, I shall continue from this podium here to defend the rights of the oppressed, the rights of the aggrieved and the voiceless. And I'll continue to be their voice, to speak on their behalf and to fight for them. If necessary, we'll endure hardship. If necessary, we'll pay the price, but we'll not remain silent in the face of injustice and we'll never consent to oppression. Now, when we look at the course of the world today, we can see that there are two paths before us. Either we'll deepen uncertainty through fear, through conflict and isolation, or we'll build the future together through justice, solidarity, and common will. Of course, it is easy to punch darkness. What is difficult is to light a candle that will dispel that darkness. Turkey has chosen the second path, and hopefully we'll follow it with patience. May God ease our way and be our guide and helper, I pray. I invite our friends listening to us in this very hall today and from every corner of the world to embrace this shared vision of the future. I greet you all with the warmest of regards on my own behalf, on behalf of my people. Until we meet again, I salute you all once with respect.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, distinguished heads of delegations, ladies and gentlemen. At the outset of my speech, I would like to sincerely congratulate Mr. Halilovic on being elected as the President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly and wish him further success. As you are all aware, last year the international community marked the 80th anniversary of the United Nations. For 80 years, this unique global organization has been standing at the forefront of safeguarding peace, security, and development. Although our organization brings together all countries of the world and serves as the principal platform for international cooperation, wars and tensions still persist in various regions. Armed conflicts and humanitarian crises in different parts of the world including Ukraine, Iran, Sudan, and Palestine, demonstrate the complexity of the current international environment and require all of us to work together to strengthen peace, security, and sustainable development. Kyrgyzstan is a country that believes in the power of dialogue and the peaceful settlement of conflicts. Our country stands ready to serve as a mediator in addressing complex and contentious issues. In recent years, Central Asia has clearly demonstrated to the world its ability to resolve complex interstate issues peacefully. Today, Central Asia is becoming an example of constructive interstate cooperation as well as economic, infrastructural, and technological development. In this regard, we are ready to share the experience we have accumulated along this path. Distinguished heads of delegations, for the first time in its history, Kyrgyzstan has been elected as a member of the United Nations Security Council for the 2027-2028 term. Taking this opportunity, I would like to express my profound gratitude to all countries that supported our candidacy. The support of 142 member states not only confirms Kyrgyzstan's readiness to contribute to international affairs, but also demonstrates the growing role of the Central Asian region in international relations. This achievement is clear evidence that even small states can make a meaningful contribution to addressing global challenges. We fully understand that membership in the Security Council is not a privilege or reward. It is a great responsibility. One year ago, standing at this stage, I started with confidence that Kyrgyzstan is among those states whose experience enables them to put forward substantive issues for consideration by the Security Council. We do not forget the promises we have made and will make every effort to implement them fully. Therefore, I would like to reiterate, Kyrgyzstan firmly adheres to international law, justice, and the protection of human rights, and supports the multilateral system based on mutual respect, balance of interest, and responsibility toward future generations. We intend to work closely with every country and remain committed to productive cooperation. Distinguished colleagues, as you all may know, since the establishment of the United Nations in 1945, its Member States and leaders have attempted to undertake systematic reforms. Reforms have ranged from expanding the membership of the Security Council to modernizing mechanisms of governance, peacekeeping, and the protection of human rights. These initiatives continue to be actively discussed at the international level. However, despite numerous efforts and years of discussion, the institutional structure of our organization continues to face various challenges. Therefore, I believe that expanding the membership of the Security Council is one of the reforms that the international community expects. I consider it fair to grant two permanent seats to the African continent with population of more than 1 billion people and one permanent seat to Latin America. Today, the world has changed. At the same time, a number of developed countries have also expressed their aspiration to become members of the Security Council. I believe that the request of these countries should be also considered. Another issue, in my view, the weakness of effective mechanisms for ensuring the implementation of the decisions of the organization. The systematic failure to implement the organization's decisions undermines the legitimacy of multilateralism concept, creates the impression that international law is not binding and encourages disregard for international obligations. Therefore, we must expand and strengthen the authority of the United Nations. In this regard, we propose to develop the United Nations mechanism for the implementation of decisions and accountability. First, it is necessary to establish within the framework of the General Assembly the permanent public registry of the implementation of resolutions and obligations by member states. This registry could include the following information and ensure the implementation of such mechanisms as: First, systematically record and verify the level of implementation of adopted decisions. Second, establish the obligation for member states to regularly submit report in accordance with the agreed standards. Third, provide analytical reviews on sectors and regions. Fourth, ensure transparency and equal access to information for all states. The registry could be administered by the United Nations Secretariat with the support of independent experts. If decisions of the Organization are systematically not implemented, I propose the gradual response mechanisms. an official notification to the concerned State, followed by consultations with the relevant bodies of the Organization. Development of a monitoring mission to the country concerned to assess the objective obstacles preventing the implementation of the decision and to prepare recommendations. The third stage, consideration of the case right here at the plenary meeting of the General Assembly to determine the status of the concerned state in terms of its systematic implementation or non-implementation of United Nations decisions. The fourth stage, the initiation of appropriate procedures under the Charter of the United Nations with regard to states that fail to comply with the requirements. In particular, the matter could be referred to the United Nations Security Council for consideration of restrictive measures provided for the international law, including: the first, temporary restriction on participation in United Nations programs; the second, recommendations to review existing formats of cooperation and other diplomatic measures where appropriate. Distinguished colleagues, I believe that when cases of systematic non-implementation of United Nations decisions are considered, the permanent members of the Security Council should voluntarily refrain from using the veto. If a mechanism designed to ensure the implementation of the organization's decisions is systematically blocked by permanent members through the use of the veto, such practice would no longer be consistent with the spirit of the UN Charter and the principle of equal responsibility of member states. Therefore, we should once again consider the possibility of voluntarily restraining to use the veto in matters related to the implementation of the organization's decisions. This approach could promote universality, the equality of all states regardless of their size, the primacy of diplomacy, and avoid the double standards. In order to implement this initiative, I propose establishing to open a working group with the General Assembly with the participation of the interested member states. The working group could conduct intergovernmental consultations and prepare a report on possible models for the proposed mechanism. Following these consultations, the General Assembly and the Security Council should consider adopting the relevant resolutions and decisions. The strategic objective of this initiative is to ensure that the decisions of the Organization are treated not merely as political recommendations, but as genuine international obligations. Improvement of their implementation would strengthen the rule of international law and reinforce confidence in the United Nations. Kyrgyzstan is ready to initiate interstate discussions on the development of such a mechanism. Starting from the 1st January 2027, as a member of the United Nations Security Council, we intend to formally submit all these proposals to the relevant committee. Distinguished colleagues, I would like to address separately the issues of sanctions. As we have all observed, today's sanctions are in some cases used by individual countries as an instrument to interference to the international affairs of sovereign states. The negative consequences of unjustified unilateral sanctions also affect small countries such as ours, which are at the stage of formation and development. In some cases, such practices led to interference into the internal affairs of independent states and contradicted the fundamental principles of international law. Some major states, in pursuit of their own interests, put pressure on smaller countries such as Kyrgyzstan, attempting to force them to bargain over certain matters and issuing ultimatums. In this context, I would like to take this opportunity to to note that the decision made by the President of the United States, His Excellency Mr. Donald Trump, after taking office, hold funding of non-governmental organizations around the world. As a result, interference by NGOs in the internal affairs and policies of the developing countries has practically ceased. President Trump's decisions have created conditions for strengthening the sovereignty of states and enabling them to independently choose their own path of development. Therefore, taking this opportunity, I would like to express my appreciation to Mr. Trump for ending the funding of the NGOs. Distinguished colleagues. Decisions to impose sanctions should be taken in accordance with the UN Charter and exclusively within the mandate of the Security Council. We believe that the mandate to impose sanctions against a state should belong exclusively to the United Nations. In my view, this is the only possible way to improve the international sanctions system. First and foremost, we should introduce mandatory mechanisms under which all sanctions and measures are reviewed in advance by organization. The prior review of sanction would help ensure that their potential humanitarian, economic, and social consequences are taken into account. An important element of the proposed mechanism should be the enhanced transparency and accountability. States initiating sanctions should clearly indicate the legal basis for such measures explain their necessity and objectives, and define clear criteria and conditions for their eventual removal. I believe it would be appropriate to establish, under the auspices of the United Nations, the unified international mechanism for monitoring sanctions and reviewing them on a regular basis. Only then can the central role of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security be strengthened and its mandate enhanced. This would also help eliminate the risk of sanctions being used arbitrarily by one country against another for political or economic gain. No state should act arbitrarily. The United Nations must be strong. Every country should tremble when the United Nations intends to impose sanctions. Only then the strict international order can be established in the world. Otherwise, some decisions of the United Nations may no longer be taken seriously, while states simply act according to their own discretion. Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay. If a state fails to implement such decisions and other countries cease cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase. Only then will decisions be implemented promptly and the United will become a strong and respected organization. Otherwise, existing sanctions will become sort of children's toy. Dear friends, as you know, climate change has become a global challenge. The average temperature of our planet and the number of climate-related emergencies are rising rapidly, while the negative impact on energy, agriculture, food security and the economy as a whole has reached a significant scale. Kyrgyzstan is a mountainous country. We are particularly vulnerable to effect of melting glaciers, and this is not an abstract threat. It is an environmental challenge of the regional significance. I believe it is extremely important and necessary to unite international efforts in addressing climate challenges and the problems facing mountainous regions. In this regard, 21st 23rd October 2027, Bishkek will host the second Global Mountain Summit, Bishkek+25. Taking this opportunity, I invite all of you to participate in the summit. The summit will serve as the concluding event for the five years of action for the development of mountain regions for 2023-2027 term. During my meeting with United Nations Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, in Bishkek on 31 August 2026, I proposed organizing this summit jointly with the Organization. These efforts demonstrate our country's leading role among mountain states and its commitment to unite international efforts to address their challenges. Therefore, Kyrgyzstan stands fully ready to serve with the United Nations as the voice of small and developing countries in addressing the climate-related challenges affecting mountainous regions. Distinguished heads of delegations, continuing the topic of climate change, I would like to draw your attention to another environmental challenge. As we all know, global problems and disasters often have their origins at the local level. The issue concerns the unique high-altitude Lake Issyk-Kul, which is the part of the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and is included among wetlands of international importance under the Ramsar framework. Today, this invaluable natural water reservoir is under severe climatic stress. Over the past 170 years, the water level has fallen by almost 14 meters, while over the past five years, the rate of decline has reached approximately 7 centimeters per year. 101 rivers historically flowed into the lake, but today only 30 flow throughout the entire year. The main source of water for Lake Issyk-Kul is the glacier of the Tian Shan Mountains. Over the past 70 years, more than 30% of the region's mountain glaciers have melted. Nearly 20% of this reduction has occurred within the just past seven to 10 years. This process poses a direct threat to the biodiversity of the region and economic stability of hundreds of thousands of people. As part of our efforts to preserve Lake Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyzstan is mobilizing all available domestic resources. In particular, the state concept for the sustainable development of the Issyk-Kul ecological and economic system until 2030 is being implemented. Strict environmental restrictions have been introduced and pilot projects have been launched to monitor the depths of the lake using the underwater robotic technologies. Large-scale efforts to clean the lake bed and its waters are continuing on a regular basis. The scale and speed of climate change exceed the capacity of any individual mountain country and require consolidated international action. The loss of Lake Issyk-Kul would not be merely a local tragedy; it would become an irreversible environmental loss for the entire region. In order to understand the potential scale of this environmental challenge and the costs associated with preventing it, it is important to look at the fate of the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, both of which have suffered severely over recent decades. Not so long ago, the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, just like Issyk-Kul today, were full and reservoir was full of water. Today, they have largely dried up. For us, this example must serve as a clear warning. Taking this opportunity, I officially call upon the United Nations, international financial institutions, and donor countries to support our initiative to establish under the auspice of the organization the special joint trust fund for the preservation of Lake Issyk-Kul. In order to demonstrate our commitments through concrete actions, we are prepared to contribute 10 million US dollars from the state budget to this fund. In our culture, there is a concept known as "amanat". It means the duty to carefully preserve what our ancestors have entrusted to us and to pass it on to future generations. In this sense, it would be fair to state that Lake Issyk-Kul is our shared climate amanat. We are not asking for help. We are proposing a joint global partnership to preserve this unique natural resource for the Earth. Before it is too late, let us unite our efforts and resources within the framework of this trust fund. Distinguished participants, ladies and gentlemen, The challenges before us are shared, therefore our response to them must be also collective. We stand at the threshold of a new era of change. Safe, just and sustainable future can be built only through collective action. The destiny of our planet and future generations is the responsibility of each and every one of us. This year, Kyrgyzstan celebrates the 31st anniversary of its independence. Throughout this period, our country has faced many different challenges. Since then, we chose cooperation over confrontation, creation over destruction, and embark upon the path of sustainable development. There is one thing we must all remember: peace does not come about by itself. Therefore, let us turn our words into action, concrete steps that improve people's lives and protect nature. Let us build together a world which dialogue is stronger than weapons, mutual respect is stronger than fear, and cooperation among nations delivers tangible results for all humanity. Thank you very much for your attention.

In the name of God, the most gracious, the most merciful, your excellency, president of the general assembly, your excellency, secretary general, ladies and gentlemen, may the peace, mercy, and blessings of God be upon you. I extend my congratulations to his excellency, mister Khalil Rahman, on his assumption of the presidency of this session, and wish him every success. It is the cumulative result of years of postponing crisis management through temporary solutions and unrealistic policies. Our perspective has always been that the way to resolve disputes is through dialogue and negotiations to reach just fair solutions grounded in international law, grounded in respect for the sovereignty of states and the rights of peoples. This remains our position in the aftermath of the wars we've been witnessing. The state of Qatar, through its role as a trusted mediator and peace facilitators, has consistently warned that time does not resolve lingering conflicts in the absence of a just settlement, rather it doubles their costs. Ladies and gentlemen, at the heart of the dangerous situation we're witnessing lies the absence of a regional system of collective security, one that respects the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of states, one that promotes the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-interference in the internal affairs of states. We have previously called from this very podium for the establishment of such a system, and we reiterate that call after recent events have demonstrated the urgent need for it. In the absence of such a system, it has become possible for a war to erupt. Owing to considerations unrelated to the interests of the countries of the region, it has become possible for one party to drag its neighbors into a war that is not theirs, targeting their vital assets and installations, despite their strenuous efforts to avert escalation. It has become possible for an international waterway, through which nearly a quarter of the world's energy trade passes, to be closed. It has also become possible for the lifelines of the global economy to be turned into tools of pressure and bargaining, with people on every continent bearing the cost, despite being far removed from the causes of the conflict. This is a crisis that drives up the prices of food and medicine and affects the livelihoods of peoples who have nothing to do with any of this. Despite all those developments, which could have been avoided. We remain deeply convinced, and our conviction is based on realistic considerations, convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, by reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation and returning to negotiations in order to avert war, paving the way toward a lasting solution that ensures security and stability for the entire region, including Iran, while opening prospects for cooperation across various fields and ensuring non-interference in the internal affairs of states. The opportunity for a peaceful diplomatic solution, which we believe is both possible and realistic, must not be missed. Your Excellencies, while we're doing everything within our power to address the situation through diplomatic efforts, we have strengthened our steadfastness to defend our sovereignty, our territory, and our people, and the foundations of normalcy. We have devised resilient, flexible economic plans and remain committed to our development projects, despite the severe adverse impact of the war and the heavy price it has exacted. At every juncture and in every crisis, we have chosen to combine resilience with flexibility and to place the interests of our nation, our people, and those residing on our soil above all else. Our values are not mere slogans we proclaim, but a reality we live by. They are values that we put into practice. At their core is the conviction that the dignity of the nation cannot be compromised. and that wisdom and firmness are two sides of the same coin. This approach is firmly anchored in our nation. This approach has been championed by the leaders of Qatar, from the founder, Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed bin Thani, to His Highness Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, our Emir from 1995 to 2013. May Allah have mercy on his soul. He passed away this year and was mourned with profound affection and gratitude by his people and all peace-loving nations people across the region and around the world. On this occasion, I would like to thank the United Nations General Assembly for convening a special session in honor of his memory and in recognition of his legacy. The experiences and challenges we have confronted have demonstrated that resilience is the outcome of prior planning, preparedness, and investment in people and national capabilities. Accordingly, over the years, We have worked on assessing risks, securing supply chains, strengthening the capabilities of our national institutions, developing strategic reserves, and forging trusted international partnerships. Recognizing the nexus of peace, security, development, human rights, and the rule of law, the State of Qatar maintains its investment in development, education, health, security, and economic diversification in conformity with the Qatar National Vision 2030.
