On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Emir of the State of Qatar. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Gitanas Nauseda, President of the Republic of Lithuania. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Your Excellency, Madam President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, 35 years ago, Lithuania returned to its rightful place in the global community of sovereign states. By joining the United Nations, we reaffirmed our strong commitment to the global order based on international law, territorial integrity, state sovereignty, and human dignity. It was a glorious moment for a nation well taught by historical experience that freedom and independence cannot be taken for granted. They must be constantly and consistently defended. Today, I am standing here to speak for the same dream that inspired Lithuania in 1991: the vision of the more just, secure, and peaceful world. Today, I am backing up the principles of the United Nations, which, sadly, are being put under increasing pressure. Recent years have brought us numerous high-intensity and far-reaching conflicts that dominate the global affairs on a scale not seen in decades. We witness geopolitical instability in Europe, the Middle East, and elsewhere. It is made worse by growing nuclear ambitions in the Middle East and Asia, as well as the irresponsible transfer of military-related goods, use items and sensitive technologies. In recent months, Iran has continued attacking neighboring countries, often through its proxies, while actively impairing the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. These actions constitute a serious threat to regional and international peace and security. We reaffirm our full solidarity with the Gulf Cooperation Council countries and Jordan. We call on Iran to halt its nuclear and missile programs, as well as its collaboration with armed groups across the Middle East. Lithuania commends all efforts to find a solution ensuring freedom of navigation. We will contribute with our demining capabilities to the international maritime missions in the Strait of Hormuz. As regards the situation in the Gaza Strip, my country supports international efforts to maintain and consolidate the ceasefire. The comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict, including the deployment of the temporary international stabilization force, provides the guidelines to follow. Lithuania reiterates the importance of full demilitarization of non-state armed groups. Humanitarian aid must also be allowed to reach those in need safely and without obstruction. To this day, the two-state solution remains the only way towards a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace. In this light, It is crucially important to abstain from any further actions incompatible with a credible political process. Ladies and gentlemen, the one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, supported by its proxies. In the 12 years since the illegal occupation of Crimea, Russia has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in eastern Ukraine to massive military operations, mass killings, and ultimately the largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen. The current stage of the war which began with the full-scale invasion in February 2022, has already lasted longer than the First World War. In the last 55 months, Russia has suffered 1.5 million military casualties. In the last year, it has gained 0.3% of Ukraine's territory at the cost of over 400,000 soldiers killed and wounded. Yet, all these enormous efforts, all that blood and tears, basically came to nothing. Ukraine is still standing proudly as an independent state. The Ukrainian language, culture, and national identity are alive and thriving. In all but name, Russia has already lost the war. Yet its leadership does not allow itself to admit defeat, fearing international legal accountability and possible revenge from its own people. As inevitable approaches, the stakes get higher and the Kremlin regime increasingly finds itself cornered. How much more Ukrainian civilian lives will be sacrificed on Russia's war altar? How many people will be tortured, sexually assaulted, thrown into dark dungeons, never to see the sunlight again? How many children will be illegally separated from their parents and sent to Russia to suffer indoctrination? We do not know the answers, yet we must all feel the deep pain brought by this brutal and pointless war. And we all should join our forces to draw Ukraine's victory closer. For it is only Ukraine's final victory, safeguarding its sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, that could ensure the global peace, security, and credibility of the United Nations Charter. What we cannot allow is the brute force prevailing over international law. We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow's colonial aspirations which undermine global food security and driving up food prices. Russia's imperial ambitions reach far into Europe, Africa, and Asia. No country should consider itself immune from this threat. Naturally, Lithuania witnesses many dangers up close. In recent months, Russia's war of aggression has led to numerous violations of our airspace, by combat drones. Russia has also intensified hybrid attacks, disinformation, and sabotage efforts. Where Russia advances, opening Pandora's box of new techniques for destabilization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas. Ladies and gentlemen, attacks on information integrity pose an especially troubling challenge to every society. Disinformation, foreign information manipulation and interference, and the falsification of history erode trust, restrict civic space, and target journalists and human rights defenders. As a result, human rights, democracy, and security suffer. This risk is further enhanced by the development of artificial intelligence. As we all know, AI has a huge potential for transformation, especially in the field of economy. Whole sectors, including those related to defense and security, might get radically changed or destroyed almost overnight. As any instrument, AI is also increasingly used by those seeking to cause harm and destruction. My country, Lithuania, strongly believes that the future of AI must not be determined by authoritarian control, technological coercion, or the malicious use of data. We are therefore investing in trusted AI capabilities, promoting responsible AI deployment, and advancing the Vilnius Convention, the world's first legally binding international treaty on artificial intelligence. By demonstrating how shared principles can be translated into concrete legal commitments, we hope to contribute significantly to the United Nations global dialogue on AI governance. Lithuania invites the international community to unite in addressing significant legal, ethical, and strategic challenges posed by artificial intelligence. With even major technology companies sending warning signals that control of AI might slip out of humanity's hands, the time is ripe for collective action. Together, we must ensure that AI serves human dignity, sustainable development, and international security, rather than becoming a new instrument of inequality, manipulation, or conflict. At any cost, human accountability, international law, and the peace and security must be safeguarded. Ladies and gentlemen, the credibility of the United Nations depends on its ability to respond firmly to aggression, unlawful conquest, forced deportations, and crimes against humanity. and also to coordinate the global response to the growth of AI. I am grateful to the Secretary-General, His Excellency Antonio Guterres, for his long-lasting service and his focus on reforming the United Nations into a more effective, modern, and responsive organization. This is the correct path to follow. There is no other way. No nation can confront today's challenges alone. Aggression cannot win. It is only through multilateralism, solidarity, and the unity of all member states that we can uphold peace, security, and the rule-based international order. It is also important to learn from the many lessons of history. Today, Too many seem unwilling to recognize and confront the past crimes committed by totalitarian regimes, including Soviet crimes. This is a fundamental flaw. We must remember the past so as not to repeat it. That is why Lithuania is promoting the concept of historical remembrance. My personal wish is to see the Pan-European Memorial to all victims of 20th century totalitarian regimes unveiled in Brussels as soon as possible. There is one lesson Lithuania, having survived and overcome numerous occupations and the waves of repression, can share with international community. Freedom can be delayed. but it cannot be extinguished. Justice can be challenged, but it cannot be defeated. This, I believe, is a message that goes far beyond an experience of the single person or the nation. It speaks to the whole humankind, united in our shared dignity. At a time of growing global uncertainty and power politics, We need even more multilateralism grounded in international law, the UN Charter, and universal human rights. We need to resist the law of the strongest collectively in order not to fall under the yoke separately. The time to act is now. And I believe, I want to believe, that we have what it takes to make the world a more just, secure, peaceful place to live. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Lithuania. The Assembly will now hear an address by Her Excellency Keiko Sofia Fujimori Higuchi, President of the Republic of Peru. I request protocol to escort Her Excellency and invite her to address the Assembly.

President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General, ladies and gentlemen, heads of state and government, distinguished delegates, I am taking the floor to address you at this global rostrum. bringing the greetings to you of an age-old civilization. We have civilizations that date back more than 5,000 years. I come from a land in which history was carved into stone and in which geographical challenges were transformed into opportunities for civilizations to meet. Centuries ago, the Incas built capacchian. a majestic network of roads that was built to meet the peoples, to bring together diverse realities, and to ensure that no corner of the empire was left isolated and forgotten. This same spirit, this spirit that seeks to bring together is the spirit that brings us here today. I am appearing at the General Assembly of the United Nations today for the first time. Only 57 days ago, I had the honor of assuming the presidency of the Republic of Peru. Mine is a proud and resilient people, and we are a founding member state of this organization. Peru comes to this Assembly reaffirming its ironclad commitment to the United Nations Charter and its fundamental principles, peace and security, development and human rights, the three pillars of the United Nations. I come from a country which is all too well aware of the high price of peace. We conquered terrorism, but regrettably, today still, after 34 years, Those who took up that mantle continue to be judged and tried, despite the fact that they have demonstrated that due process was violated. Peru, as other Latin American countries, has seen agendas imposed upon us that have divided us as a society. Politics have been instrumentalized. Democracy has been eroded, and the institution of the family has been weakened, an institution that is so crucial for the Peruvian people. The United Nations must continue to stand as the meeting place par excellence for our peoples, a meeting place which respects diverse realities and traditions. always within the framework of peace, development, and human rights. Consequently, we express our hope that we will seek to rebuild trust, and we hope that in that endeavor, the United Nations will act independently, impartially, and show that it has a true vocation for dialogue. The United Nations must show us that it can forge paths, including and even when understanding seems impossible to achieve. Let us seek to grow stronger and fly the flag of the very raison d'etre of this organization, that is to find common ground on common issues, including when we hold different opinions. After more than three decades in my country's policies, I can bear witness to how the Peruvian people have endured periods, or rather experienced periods, of intense hope in which trust in democratic institutions and governments has actually grown stronger. We have forged ahead because, in addition to defeating terrorism, we have proven able to almost triple, in real terms, our GDP. We have multiplied 15-fold the value of our exports, and we have ensured that our currency is now among the most stable in the world. Despite this progress, the most recent governments were not capable of addressing new challenges or of closing the social divides which continue to remain in Peru. We continue to have structural problems that need to be resolved, problems that stymie more uniform development. divides and problems which erode citizens trust in democratic institutions and authorities. Allow me to share with you, ladies and gentlemen, some of the most pressing challenges that Peru is currently facing. The first major challenge we face is the frontal assault we must wage on organized crime and petty crime. Peru is located on a continent in which there are no wars between nations. However, we are faced with another type of war, that is that declared by transnational criminal organizations, organizations that have sowed terror among our people. In this war, There are no battle grounds, no fronts. Indeed, no fronts have been defined. There are no international rules governing these conflicts. The enemy does not wear a uniform. The enemy hides among our people. There is no possibility to see surrender or to sign peace treaties. In this context, confronting this war as an isolated problem to be dealt with by each nation alone is not only mistaken thinking and a mistake that we've been making, rather it is an act of giving the advantage to transnational organized crime. To make that mistake allows them to grow stronger. They have huge economic and warmongering power. And they get that through crimes and illegal businesses that range from smuggling, illegal mining, drug trafficking, human trafficking, extortion, and killing. Consequently, the first thing we must do is isolate or pinpoint and identify the enemy. These organisations, these enemies are terrorist groups and they must be tackled for as what they are. They are enemies of a democratic state and of fine upstanding citizens. Clearly defining what who the enemy is and establishing a normative framework will allow the armed forces in supporting the national police to act with resolve and tackle the threat to the domestic order posed by these organizations. Moreover, in addition to actively participating in the regional Santiago Pact, Peru recently joined the Shield of the Americas. That was a demonstration of its decisive commitment to working together and in concert with our partners in this challenge, which is of the utmost priority for Peru. In Peru, we will pursue crime and prosecute it. We'll go after the man that commits the crimes and go after the network that supports him. We will not waver in the face of those that attempt to impose terror over and above the law. Suppressing, repressing these organizations, we'll do that with the full force of the law, but doing that is not enough. if at the same time we do not tackle the challenge that is developing a better educational system. There need to be effective opportunities for learning for our children and young people. It's only through providing those that young people and adults can enter the labour markets instead of being recruited by criminal groups. Consequently, our second challenge will be that of making education a tool for social transformation and a tool for the prevention of violence and crime. The quality of education. and the depth of learning enjoyed by our children and young people is a predictor of higher a higher quality of life because such education make it possible to develop higher income, better health habits and that serves the cause of social mobility. On the other hand, we've noted that shortcomings and weak points in our education system combined with other factors to predict crime and indeed fuel crime. With that in mind, my government has launched a wholesale reform of the Peruvian education system. This reform will strengthen educational infrastructure. It will increase the provision of digital learning and the provision of educational material. We will also bolster the resources given to teachers to teach. At the heart of our reform will be the creation of a headteacher training school. The goal is to equip headteachers with the tools and skills they need to lead their schools independently so that schools can become inspiring models that promote the participation of parents in this mission that is that of making every child a citizen that stands in solidarity with others, respects them and a citizen proud of their country. I must recognize that an ideological cultural agenda that is not in line with our reality and the imposition of it has sowed confusion and disorder of such magnitude that today teachers in our schools are not able to keep order in the classroom. They cannot discipline their classes because they cower under the threat of being reported. We need to re-establish the principle of respect for authority. We will make our classrooms safe spaces in which children go to learn and teachers go to teach without fear. This is our agenda. It is not that of anyone else being imposed. The role of a state is to withdraw unfair barriers, barriers that stymie people's development. We intend to provide people with the conditions they need to thrive. Effort, talent and freedom, as shown by everybody, should then do the rest. Our third major challenge is that of strengthening our institutions and our democracy. In Peru, we believe in the freedom of individuals. We believe in the family as an irreplaceable pillar of our society. We believe in respecting tradition. We believe in equality before the law and human dignity. And of course, we believe in the new name of peace, that is justice. The fact is that in our quest to ensure that freedom can be fully exercised by all, we have to underscore the overriding need for a judiciary which imposes the law in full respect of due process and individual freedoms. Consequently, Peru is of the view that genuine democracy is achieved with respect for the independence and autonomy of powers, firm justice, ironclad justice, which is truly impartial and committed to due process. The defense of human rights must not ultimately turn victims into those in the dock and torturers into those we protect. The rights of citizens must begin when impunity of the torturer comes to an end. As such, it is up to the international community to act with the same resolve in the face of any and all violations when we are at our most vulnerable. Peruvians don't always find a place within the international community or the empathy that they need or loyalty to the principles that gave rise to this General Assembly. The fact is that the international community really acquires true logic and meaning when it manages to be present at the most critical, difficult junctures. The international community must act within its own limits and ensure there is a community of sovereign nations. Supporting a country does not mean replacing its institutions or overriding the decisions that it is up to its citizens to make within the democratic order. We can share universal principles and at the same time recognize that every people has its own story, its own history, its own culture, its own traditions, and the legitimate right to democratically define its own path. We hope to see independent, transparent action which does not make ideological calculations and without those calculations manages to respect and ensure all human rights, the rights of peasants, children, women, the rights of police forces and members of the military that are on the front line in the defence of life and freedom. This forum has before it the historic duty to be a space for the meeting, the coming together of equals, a place for genuine cooperation, free of external diktats and attempts to standardise and homogenise thought. Those of us that come from nations that are constantly having to recover and get back on their feet, we come here today absolutely sure of the fact that we can share great principles without ever turning our back on what we are. We do not need to all think in the same way to have deep mutual respect for one another. The world does not require identical democracies. It requires legitimate democracies. It does not demand nations that are all the same. It does not need cookie cutter nations. It means needs truly free peoples. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Peru. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Jose Antonio Kast, President of the Republic of Chile. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

A very, very good afternoon to you all. Secretary-General, President of the General Assembly, Heads of State and Government, distinguished delegates. Particular greetings to the delegation that has travelled with me from Chile. I wish to greet our Minister for Foreign Affairs, our Minister for the Environment, for Development and the Family, our ambassadors, our senators and members of Parliament. And I wish to greet each and every Chilean person. Greetings and a warm embrace to you all. 64 years ago in this same forum, the then President of Chile, Jorge Alessandri, described our country, Chile, as a large, narrow nation between the Andes and the Pacific, extending from there till the moving expanse of the Antarctic. The land remains where it is. What has changed is the world around it. What has changed first and foremost is Chile. For the vast swathes of the '90s and until the beginning of the 2000s, Chile was a success story and a model for many regions and nations. Our country implemented economic policies that prioritized economic stability, openness to trade, and private investment. In the Latin American context, in which many nations were facing inflation crises and external debt, Chile distinguished itself because it continued to show fiscal responsibility, display high rates of growth and poverty reduction. What happened then? Chile ground to a halt. Things stagnated. It took bad decisions. Public policies were implemented that increased taxation, regulation, and obstacles to entrepreneurship. We also weathered a very difficult juncture in October 2019. Chile then fell to its knees in our streets. For months, there was an outbreak of violence, chaos reigned and disorder prevailed. All of that brought consequences with it. Investment plummeted, employment ground to a standstill and homicide levels rose to an extent that Chile had never seen in modern history as a result of the rising tide of organised crime. And that all happened until very recently, until now. distinguished, I've come to this forum to tell you that Chile is back. And that is no slogan. It is the very reality of a country that today begins to stride towards development. Our government took office with one conviction. Order does not run counter to freedom. Order is one of the preconditions of freedom, the freedom to walk home worry-free and to not be a victim of crime, the freedom to run a business and not be stymied by the action of the state, the freedom to invest. and not find ourselves in a situation where the rules of the game are continually changing. We have been in government for six years and we're getting our house in order. Today, Chile is a safer, more competitive country and a nation with far less red tape. Chile is a safer country. In Chile, in the first six months of this year, the rate of homicides decreased to the tune of 11.5%. And we are now approaching pre-pandemic homicide levels. our borders are under better control. We have our border shield plan and that has made it possible to induce irregular entry by 86% and we have deported 50% more people than we did last year. People do not come in through the window; they come in through their ports with all their documents in order. In the same vein, we have the Santiago Accord. Here, I thank our Minister for Foreign Affairs, who was the person who spearheaded that initiative. This is a security initiative. Many South American nations have acceded to it so that we can coordinate to effectively combat transnational organized crime. work is not yet done, it has only just started. A safer country is a country with more trust, and where there is trust, there is more growth, employment and investment. We are also today a more competitive nation. Only a few weeks ago, Chile adopted the most significant economic reform of recent decades. approved a reduction to business tax. It's now gone from 27 to 23%. This tax had only been on the increase since 1990. It had never decreased. We have also temporarily reduced housing purchase tax, and we have launched an initiative for capital repatriation. There's better tax stability too. We now have less red tape. We are also dismantling what we call this ideology of always having to issue permits. This is, if you like, a sort of hidden bureaucracy which stops business projects from forging ahead in six months. In the last six months, we've had requests to invest more than $44 billion in our economy. And these investment projects applications are being assessed by our environmental evaluation systems. More than $33 billion have been approved for projects that had been in the wings for years. We have only $17 billion for environmental projects. We are taking tangible actions that are changing the very course of Chile and bringing us closer to development. The economy is not yet taking off and unemployment is still plunging thousands of families into anguish, but... Unemployment is hard and high, but it will change. Change will come. Results are slow to materialise, but structural reforms are under way. We know where we are going, and we are not simply reacting without having any clear course in mind. After storms, the sun always comes out. After winter, spring always arrives and after years of deadlock, Chile is back. There are many reasons that can explain how we got to where we are, but there's only one path that we need to follow for Chile to once again take off, spread its wings and fly. That is the path of unity. Unity between all of those that defend freedom and want to see Chile's people thrive. There are many things that might separate the right and the left in Chile, but we are united by our desires to see Chile grow once more and become a safer nation. Delegates, people from the investment world are listening to us, and I say to you, choose Chile to invest. You will find clear rules that do not change day-to-day. You will find courts that function, contracts that are abided by, and a state ready to facilitate investment. Chile understands that in a multipolar world, institutional stability is not a luxury, it is a need. For example, we are a pioneer in the energy transition. Chile possesses around a quarter of global lithium reserves, and we are the largest producer of copper on the planet. Chile has a lot of sunlight, the heat of the sun, a long Pacific coast, lakes. rivers, volcanoes that can create vast stores of energy. Chile also has the Strait of Magellan, a crucial alternative route for global trade. Our nation will become the bridge and the port for the bio-oceanic corridors that will unite America with Asia. This richness, this wealth, is not only fortune that we have in our coffers, it brings with it responsibility to you. Chile will never renounce its sovereignty, neither will it to exploit its own minerals. At the same time, we have our sovereignty, of course, but at the same time, we say that the energy of the future must serve humankind, and energy must not be held hostage by monopolies or actors that do not abide by the rules. Please make no mistake here, it is possible to reconcile growth and sustainability. The two are inseparable. Chile understands that environmental protection and economic progress form part of one single development strategy, one in which investment and innovation are linchpins when it comes to improving the quality of life of our people. Sustainable development requires robust institutions, clear rules, timely decisions and effective administration, able to turn commitments and diagnoses into tangible results for both people and the environment. President, I now wish to turn to a discussion of our continent, Latin America, because I sincerely believe that the coming decade can be ours. For the first time in a long time, Latin American governments are really, truly uniting and working together, not by simply issuing communiques, but getting to know each other and speaking to each other to really come up with common plans against transnational organized crime, migration control, and coming together to forge joint development opportunities. Latin America is the continent of the future, and those of us that lead the continent today are ready to give momentum to that change. Relations with our neighbors, Peru, Bolivia, and Argentina are in fine fettle. We are resuming relations with Venezuela under a new leadership. We've opened doors that were closed for years. Some people will say to us that we don't, or they don't, understand this change, but others or that they don't understand this move on our part. Others will say that we're simply new, unthinking allies of this country, but we're neither one or the other. We recognise the reality for what it is. We value change where it exists and we offer support. We're of the view that Venezuela has before it a historic opportunity to reconcile with its best democratic traditions, with its institutions and with the millions of its children that are now scattered across our continent that want to return. This path will be a Demanding one, Chile is ready and willing to provide the help necessary. After two decades of tensions, Latin America wants this history to have a happy conclusion. Delegates, this Assembly cannot remain indifferent to the wars and conflicts that are raging around the world. These open conflicts do not only threaten the stability of many regions, rather they damage the entire world. Chile, like many countries represented in this Chamber, imports almost all of the oil it consumes and has been directly affected by manifold wars. I'm not talking here about abstract geopolitics. The impact is expressed in the cost of bread, transport and harvest, inflation that refuses to hold still, taxes that do not decrease, investment delayed and jobs that don't arrive, entire countries that were really taking off and triumphing have once again ground to a halt and seen stagnation settle in for wars that they didn't start and that they can't stop. For therefore, our appeal to you is direct. Wars must stop. Wars do not only drain the blood of those that fight them, they plunge people into poverty. Indeed, they do that for the whole world. We all lose with wars and we've lost too much. The United Nations has a role to play and it must do so with the character and the dynamism that it has not yet shown. Delegates, here is the most uncomfortable thing I came to say, the hardest pill to swallow in my speech. This organization has not been commensurate with the challenges of our times. It's not only a leadership problem, one of the present or the future, but rather a problem in terms of action. For decades and for several reasons, the United Nations has not been part of the solution to the problems I've outlined. We cannot simply continue to play by the same rules of an order that was established in 1945. In 2026, what we've seen is the development of a UN architecture that holds too many discussions and is too quick to act, a Security Council that reflects the political arena of 1945 and not the reality of 2026. We have red tape that continues to proliferate, as is true for, indeed, many countries. We're seeing agendas that, however noble they might appear, have ultimately postponed what this organization committed to do with the with its founding charter that is maintain peace protect right life and defend the freedom of its peoples we believe in the United Nations and believing in the United Nations means ensuring that the organization discharges its mandate I propose three things reducing bureaucracy and focusing resources where there are lives at stake. We must suspend agendas that are not priorities to return the spotlight to those that really are priorities. We must reform the Security Council, not as a symbolic gesture, but as a vital prerequisite to ensure that the Council's decisions are once again respected and upheld. Chile signed the San Francisco Charter and has been present, ready, and willing to defend all its causes. all of its causes rather. We are committed to the high seas agreement known as the BBNJ and we proposed Valparaiso as the headquarters of its executive secretariat. That means that we now have the first UN body to ever have had a headquarters in Latin America and this is an agreement which brings together many different sectors in Chile to play this role. This housing of this headquarters is an expression of the multilateralism that we believe in, a tangible, ambitious, and able to prove to yield results. There needs to be a multilateralism that is effective and efficient. And allow me to say that the reforms I talked about cannot wait. While we discuss how to modernize institutions created in 1945, we're seeing the emergence of the most powerful technology that humankind has ever known, and no one is governing it. Artificial intelligence is not only a technical matter that we can delegate to experts. It is an ethical challenge and a geopolitical issue. We reject the false dilemma between innovation and responsibility. We do not believe that going quicker is always better, and neither are we going to turn our back on opportunities as a result of fear. our country AI can amount to and mean growth of between 10% and 20%. As such, we are choosing the path that we call responsible, one of responsible pace. That means making progress as quickly as our ability to administer progress allows. We have regulations that make things possible that do not hamper progress. We have investment in talent and in energy, and we have rigorous assessments of everything that is happening. We want to lead from a position of knowledge and not fear. And I say this in this room for one reason. The United Nations must be able to bring humankind together to discuss a technology that will decide the fate of this century. Nothing can simply be resolved by an algorithm. Mr. President, allow me to go back to the beginning. The president that I talked about that spoke here 74 years ago, spoke on behalf of his people and discarded ideological differences. He said that Chile will continue working fervently and with deep belief in the principles of the UN Charter and the fact that they must be tangibly expressed. We believe in human rights. And at that time, in 1945, we had 7 million inhabitants. Today, we have 20 million. The world has changed, and we have too. But what he said remains relevant. And once again, I say before you that Chile has come back to establish order. With order, freedom returns, trust returns, and it has done. We are Investment has returned and investment brings work. Chile is getting back on its feet as quickly as it fell, and it's come to say to the world that a country can recover, and a country recovers with votes, agreements, laws, and results. But I have one more thing to say, that is that a future can be built without being held hostage by others' decisions. Latin America can be the continent of the coming decade, not because someone gives it permission to be just that, but because we have the desire and the ability to be that country and that continent. We want to lead the path to that goal. Chile is back. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Chile. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Alexander Stubb, President of the Republic of Finland. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Madam President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, let me just begin by paying tribute to the lady that is sitting right behind me, Ambassador Elina Kalkku. She is the Finnish UN representative and she has had an

wonderful 44-year career in the Finnish diplomatic service, and she will retire in the month of October, and I would like to thank her for her services. And of course, with her President speaking here, you never know whether this will be the low point or the high point of her career. Be that as it may, former Secretary-General Kofi Annan once said, and I quote, "Whatever our differences, we stand or fall together." End of quote. When we forget this wisdom of Kofi Annan, disorder is what happens. Last year, from this very podium, I stated that foreign policy is based on three pillars: values, interests, and power. This year, I come with something much simpler: a choice, a choice between cooperation or conflict. In today's world, cooperation is undermined by a lack of trust, disregard for rules, and the weakening of institutions. And we've heard that in so many speeches here today. Conflicts are spreading, bringing suffering, violence, and injustice. According to some accounts, there are currently 65 active armed conflicts more than at any time since the end of the Cold War. Now, competition will always be there. Nations compete now harder than they did a generation ago. This doesn't worry me. What does is that more and more of them now compete against the rules on which the international order rests. So, this speech defends these rules and it calls for cooperation, it calls for multilateralism. Small nations need it to survive, and large nations need it to be great. Upholding the most basic rules, values, and institutions is our best option to ensure that competition does not escalate into conflict and that cooperation gains ground. Now, I want to begin by analyzing how the world is changing today. And as a pragmatic Finn, I will always try to deal with the world as it is because it often helps in building a world that I wish we would have. In other words, a world which we can build together. I will then make a few suggestions about what we should do next. So here we go. I think we should all be steadfast defenders of multilateralism. As Strobe Talbott reportedly remarked, "Multilateralism is hell and can be a real pain in the neck, but it is the best option for humanity as a whole." We need multilateralism in order to address our shared agenda, ranging from conflicts and climate change to sustainable development and artificial intelligence. Currently, however, we seem to be going the other way. more towards a non-cooperative and multipolar world order. This order, as it turns out, is based on zero-sum deals, transactions, and unrestrained power. This is a short-sighted approach. Tempting as it may be for some, such a multipolar order will ultimately lead to conflict. It will turn against us, whether you represent a great power, a middle power, or a small state like Finland. Between these two approaches, there's, of course, a third option, plurilateralism. It means building ad hoc coalitions when global cooperation is unattainable. And this is my first observation today, the emergence of flexible forms of cooperation around different themes and interests, be it in the economy, climate, defense, or technology. Coalition building can be a force of good, but with one condition. It should not challenge multilateralism, but build on it. It should support the UN system, not substitute it. The Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine is particularly close to my heart. It's a group of countries working to end Russia's war of aggression. The war is unlawful, unjustified, and unprovoked. Its solution will have far-reaching consequences for Ukraine and beyond. It is really about upholding international rules. The coalition works for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the UN Charter. It seeks to uphold the basic tenets of the international order. My second observation is that everywhere I travel around the world, I hear the word realignment. Realignment. Whether it is in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, or the Americans, nations are seeking new alliances and partnerships. This is a logical consequence in times of uncertainty and transformation. You seek security where you can get it. We're seeing an intensification of regional integration, akin to what we saw in the immediate aftermath of World War II. Regional organizations like the African Union, Gulf Cooperation Council, Mercosur, ASEAN, or the EU, build trust. When integration is not feasible, other forms of cooperation can prove essential. We Finns are happy to point out the historic signing of the Helsinki Final Act in 1975. It brought together 35 nations in the midst of the Cold War and laid the foundations for what would later become the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. Why do I give this example? Because at the time, there was no trust. There were deep disagreements and outright hostility. Yet, there was room for a process that reduced tensions and built common ground. I believe regions such as the Middle East, where conflicts are raging today, may consider something similar. Even in the face of conflict and grievance, a region may be able to agree on principles that foster cooperation and prevent further conflict. My third observation is that a new economic world order is taking shape. Instruments once used for economic integration, such as trade, technology, energy, investment, and supply chains, have become instruments of geopolitical competition. There was perhaps a time, at times, a naive belief that interdependence would bring about stability and peace. Now, the focus on opportunities has been replaced by the focus on threats. We've entered a world of coercion where dependencies are vulnerabilities. Countries seek choke points that can be weaponized to pressure others. But dependencies are complex. No nation, not even the biggest ones, can go it alone. All coercive actions come at a cost. And even if a mightier state dominates in the one domain, a smaller state can respond in another. In the new geopolitical environment, the economic order of the post-World War II era is seeking new forms. A new order must be based on a realistic understanding of the power balance in the world. We in the West must acknowledge that the global South and East are an expanding economic and political force. Many nations around the world have made remarkable advances in competence and know-how. We should put this collective expertise to work for the global common good. Countries are right to be wary of dangerous dependencies, but our focus on the threats should not lead us to abandon cooperation. We should strive for an economic world order built on institutions and agreements. Multilateralism is also needed in the global economy. Now, this was the first part. It's all good and well to diagnose the problem. In other words, too many nations now compete at the expense of basic rules, and that is why the world has slipped into disorder. But it matters more to find a prescription which would bring us back to order, stability, and cooperation. Thus, I will offer you three remedies for a world in disorder. To begin with, we need to go back to the basics of international law. On my recent visit to India, I came across a quote from Mahatma Gandhi, and I quote, "The breach of one rule inevitably leads to the breach of other rules," end of quote. These words resonate all too strongly today. So there is a kick-on effect of breaking the rules. We've moved back to a world defined by raw power and self-interest. Rules and values seem to be taking a backseat. Some are ready to throw in the towel, prepared to accept the defeat of the international rules-based order. That is an exaggeration. International law has been questioned and challenged before. It has never been a perfect system. But we must admit that we are at a critical juncture. Fundamental norms are being questioned in a way that erodes confidence in the entire multilateral system. Therefore, the first remedy for a world in disorder is rule of law. Today, international norms are often presented as an obstacle to the pursuit of national interest. This is both wrong and dangerous. International law has never been merely an effort to achieve universal justice, but neither can it be reduced to a mere instrument of domination. It is not only about values nor about interest. but about both. Despite the rhetoric, no major power is likely to give up its ability to shape the rules. That's why we see major powers still engaged here in the United Nations. Even when actors claim to abandon the rules, they rather seek to replace existing rules with ones more to their liking. Therefore, we will not face a world without rules. but we could be facing a world with less predictability, less restraint, a world based on rules that are more permissive for the powerful. For the collective benefit of the nations in this hall, we should continue to defend the rule of law and uphold its most fundamental principles. They include independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of nations, freedom of navigation at sea, and accountability for the most serious international crimes. The second remedy is about humanitarian principles, many of which have been mentioned in the speeches here today. The world today has an unprecedented capacity to meet humanity's most pressing needs. Since the establishment of the United Nations, poverty has declined, Access to basic education has expanded, literacy has increased, and child mortality has fallen. Yet, we are witnessing tyranny, disregard for the vulnerable, and violence against civilians in many parts of the world. Poverty and distress are still widespread. For example, Sudan is devastated by war. Millions have been displaced, and many face famine. For example, Gaza continues to be one of the world's most acute humanitarian emergencies, marked by mass displacement, the destruction of infrastructure, and the lack of essential services. For example, Haiti struggles with armed violence and extreme weather events, causing a displacement crisis, a hunger crisis, and a health crisis. We must not grow indifferent to wars and human suffering, but instead channel our efforts into preventing conflicts, upholding human rights, and strengthening sustainable economies. Our growing material prosperity should not come at the expense of our ethical responsibilities. Now, the third and final remedy is about language. In other words, how we treat each other. Unfortunately, there's no shortage of examples of those who use dismissive language to describe others and entire groups of people. Too often, those with the most provocative rhetoric receive the greatest visibility. Provocation is rewarded with attention, excess is misinterpreted as courage, and exaggeration as truth. Language can foster cooperation, but it can also break the trust and turn competition into conflict. The recipe is simple but necessary. Avoid polarization, strengthen trust, and listen to others. We need a dignified foreign policy, and that starts here in the United Nations. Now, ladies and gentlemen, let me conclude with the following remarks. I would like to thank Secretary-General Guterres for his service and his dedication to reforming and rationalizing the UN system. This work must continue. Every Secretary-General is shaped both by their era and by their own actions. And I was reminded of this when I recently read the biographies of two former Secretaries-General, U Thant and Kofi Annan, both highly influential leaders who navigated an era of great power tensions. Let me put forward a few suggestions for the new Secretary-General's consideration, whoever she may be, and for the international community at large. Now, since my first speech here two years ago, I've consistently called for a reformed Security Council. The world has changed and so should the UN. There should be at least two new permanent seats for Africa, two for Asia Pacific, and one for Latin America. No single state should have veto power, and if a member of the Security Council violates the UN Charter, its voting rights should be suspended. The world needs a functioning UN Security Council. To move forward, we need to break the impasse and be open for creative solutions. The need for reform also extends to the global economic architecture. It must be updated to reflect today's power balance. We have to make sure that international economic cooperation continues to be rules-based, legitimate, and representative. Multilateral solutions are needed in an increasingly multipolar world. We must also bring the United Nations back to peace mediation. The Secretary-General as mediator in chief will have a key role. The UN's legitimacy as a mediator is unique. Together, the UN and its member states can accomplish what neither can achieve alone. The UN needs to be at the center of rulemaking and institution building. Regional integration and thematic coalitions can and should support it. Now, let me finish by saying that artificial intelligence is the most consequential technology in the history of mankind. It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity. Humans can and should be in the driver's seat. We have a choice. We can compete, cooperate, or slow down. For me, cooperation is the best way forward. This is why Norway and Finland have, together with leaders from nations around the world, launched a call for companies, governments, regional organizations, and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier AI models. And I would really like for as many UN member states as possible to join this initiative. My country, Finland, wants the United Nations to succeed and will remain strongly engaged in its work. Therefore, we are standing for an election to the Security Council from 2029 to 2030. We are motivated by our belief in the UN Charter and the values it stands for. We will prioritize peace, people, and partnerships. We are willing to take on the responsibility of the Council membership at a time that calls for more peace. We want people and nations to thrive. We believe in dialogue and cooperation. Finally, let me make a procedural proposal. The foundations of the United States were built in San Francisco over 80 years ago. Today, we must restore balance to the world order. We must recommit to the fundamental principles of the international order, and we must embrace cooperation over conflict. What the world needs now is a new San Francisco moment, a moment where the world leaders come together to chart a way forward. A process to achieve this should start with a new Secretary-General. Thank you very much.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Finland. The Assembly will hear an address by His Royal Highness Grand Duke Guillaume of Luxembourg. I request protocol to escort His Royal Highness and invite him to address the Assembly.

Madam President, Excellencies, first and foremost, allow me to extend my warmest congratulations to His Excellency Dr. Kalliloh Raman on his election as President of the General Assembly. He can certainly count on Luxembourg's full support throughout his tenure. Madam President, the theme that has been chosen for this General Debate can hardly be more timely. When I try to paint an honest picture of the world we live in, one thing strikes me in particular. Trust is under growing strain. Trust between nations, trust between people, and perhaps most importantly, trust in our ability to work together. And yet, I believe that trust is precisely where we should begin. Not because trust is easy, but because every lasting achievement of the international community has begun with a decision to trust. This is my first address to this Assembly as Head of State of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg. I assumed office less than a year ago, It is therefore a particular honor to stand before you today and to reaffirm from this podium the importance Luxembourg attaches to the United Nations and to a rule-based international order grounded in the rule of law. But this moment also makes me reflect on what the United Nations means from the perspective of my own generation. As a relatively young man who has had the privilege of traveling the world, I have been fortunate to meet people from very different cultures, backgrounds, and traditions. These experiences have left me with a simple and lasting conviction. We can learn a lot from each other. And I remain convinced that it is only by working together that we can overcome the many challenges our world is facing today. This conviction is not naive. I am fully aware of the difficulties confronting us. But precisely because the world is becoming more difficult, I believe we must resist the temptation to give up on cooperation. There has never been a time when communication between people in different parts of the world was so easy. Millions of young people have virtual friends and acquaintances across continents through social media, gaming, and countless other forms of connection. We have never been so connected, and yet we seem increasingly unable to trust one another. This should make us reflect. Is it still possible to build a world order in which respect and the willingness to work towards common goals can prevail over the pursuit of self-interest and power? I believe it is, but it will require determination, dialogue, and a willingness to look beyond immediate interests. And this is why the United Nations matters. Madame President, Luxembourg has believed in this principle from the very beginning. 81 years ago, still deeply marked by the horrors of the Second World War, Luxembourg was among the 51 founding members that came together in San Francisco to lay the foundations of a new international order. At the time, we were the smallest country represented. We have prospered in the peace that Europe enjoyed for decades after 1945. And we have never forgotten that the peace could not be taken for granted. It was built generation after generation by those who chose cooperation over confrontation. Today, that peace is being challenged once again. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has brought war back to our continent. It is a stark reminder that peace requires constant commitment and that the principles on which our international order was built must be defended. The United Nations itself was born from that choice. Its charter called upon us to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security, and above all, to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. 81 years later, that promise is under considerable pressure. But it has not failed. Multilateralism may be imperfect, but disenchantment should lead us to reform, not to dismissal. The question is therefore not whether we still need multilateralism. The question is whether we have the courage to make it better.

Madame President, this brings me to a question that is very dear to my heart. What kind of world do we want to bequeath to future generations? We often talk about young people as if they came from the future. Truth be told, they are already shaping the present. Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to ask ourselves if we're really preparing a future that is going to earn their trust. My personal experience has done nothing but reinforce this conviction. This year, I had the privilege of succeeding His Majesty King Carl Gustaf of Sweden as honorary chair of the World Scout Foundation. My longstanding commitment to the Scout movement has taught me a great deal about the power of intergenerational dialogue, solidarity, and the values of the Scout movement. also taught me something absolutely fundamental. Placing our trust in young people means giving them responsibilities, allowing them to take action. They're growing up in a world in which there are extraordinary possibilities, but it's also a world where uncertainty runs deep. Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are already transforming our way of life and the way in which we work. The enthusiasm they give rise to also goes hand in hand with the very real concerns. The current debates about the most extreme risks of AI remind us that technological progress cannot be divorced from responsibility. As we confront these transformations, we should endow our young people with the means to develop their critical thinking skills and their creativity. And this is exactly what education is supposed to do, transmit knowledge and competencies, but also to teach young people to call things into question, to open up to others and to shoulder your responsibilities. Against this backdrop, I believe that we should have one guiding principle. Human beings should be at the heart of all of our decision making. We must protect the rights, security and the well-being of all. We should also listen to young people, ask them what we can build working hand in hand. Through different cultures and generations, I saw for myself everything that young people are capable of accomplishing when we give them our trust, we give them responsibilities and the necessary space to take action, as well as when we encourage them to work together. This is why Luxembourg supports the UN's Youth Delegate Programme as well as the United Nations Youth Office. It is also why our commitment to education, science and culture remains so important, in particular through our term on the Executive Board of UNESCO for the period 2025-2029. It is precisely these qualities which allow trust to flourish. Madam President, Luxembourg's commitment to the United Nations is underpinned by all three pillars: peace and security, human rights and development. Solidarity must be translated into deeds. We continue to allocate 1% of our national income to development cooperation. We are also building long-term partnerships with vulnerable countries. We remain committed to the multilateral humanitarian system, as well as to all those who are providing assistance where it is most needed. The same level of responsibility applies to peace and security. Conflicts affect all human beings, women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, as well as people who are already vulnerable. Protecting civilians and defending human rights cannot take a back seat to other considerations. Luxembourg has unstintingly worked to contribute to this effort through peacekeeping operations, humanitarian interventions, protecting children affected by armed conflict, the women, peace and security agenda, as well as the mine clearance humanitarian activities in Ukraine. The experience we gained as an elected member of the Security Council in 2013 and 2014 showed us that elected members can make a real difference, especially when the permanent members of the Security Council are divided. It is for this reason that Luxembourg is asking for Member States to place their trust in it as it seeks a Security Council seat for the 2031-2032 period. We do this humbly, but firm in our conviction, our conviction that a small country can offer up a different perspective, can bring different positions closer together and help find common ground when this is particularly difficult. It is the same conviction which guides our commitment to human rights. At a time when respect for human rights is being subjected to growing pressures, we must resist the temptation to see it as something that's up for discussion. Human rights are neither a privilege reserved for the few, nor the expression of one culture, of one political system. They are the very bedrock of human dignity. Our commitment is also concrete. As a member of the Human Rights Council for the period 2022-2024, Luxembourg took the full measure of just how important it is to defend human rights through multilateralism. We continue to support the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as efforts aimed at clarifying the fate of persons who disappeared in Syria.

Madam President, restoring trust also means making our institutions worthy of that trust. The Security Council must become more representative, more effective, and more accountable to the entire membership of the United Nations, Africa in particular. and it was said many times today, should have a stronger voice. And when the Security Council is paralyzed, the General Assembly must be able to play its rightful role. The United Nations must reform so that it can deliver more effectively, particularly when resources are constrained. But reform must never become an end in itself. The purpose of institutions is to serve people. Ultimately, the test of multilateralism is not how many resolutions we adopt or how many meetings we hold. It's whether a child is safer because of our decisions, whether a young person can receive an education, whether a family can live in dignity, whether a small country can believe that international law will protect it when power alone cannot. This is why trust matters. And this is why Luxembourg will continue to defend multilateralism. Because we know what happens when it fails. Madam President, Climate change reminds us perhaps more clearly than any other challenge that we cannot solve global problems by acting alone. It transcends borders and generations. Small island developing states already experiences consequences that threaten their very existence. Luxembourg may be landlocked, but we are deeply committed to this common effort including by drawing on the expertise of our financial center in green finance. Our interests may differ, but our future is shared. Madam President, the world is becoming more fragmented. The international order is under strain. We need to recognize this reality, but we should not mistake a world of competing centers of power for a more just or stable international order? For Luxembourg, the answer is clear. Our experience has taught us that international law and multilateral institutions give countries, whatever their size, a voice and place at the table. It is not about resisting a changing world, but to make multilateralism fit for that world. I believe this is ultimately what the United Nations asks of us. Not that we agree on everything, not that we abandon our national interests, but that we recognize that there are challenges for which no nation, however powerful, can find lasting solutions alone. We can look at the imperfections of multilateralism and conclude that it no longer works. Or we can reform it fairly, strengthen it, and make it worthy of the trust that future generations will place in us. I know which choice I want to make, because this is the world I want to leave to my children. A world where dialogue is stronger than confrontation, where respect between nations allows differences to become sources of strength rather than division, where international law protects the weak as well as the strong. If we restore trust, if we listen to the next generation, and if we have the courage to act together, The United Nations can continue to be more than a reflection of the world as it is. It can remain an instrument for building the world we want to leave behind, a world worthy of the trust of those who will inherit it. Young people do not expect us to solve every challenge, but they do expect us to try. They expect us to act with responsibility. And above all, they expect us not to lose faith in our ability to shape a better future. And that is the promise we should make to the next generation. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Grand Duke of Luxembourg. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Emmanuel Macron, President of the French Republic. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Madame President, Deputy Secretary-General, Majesties, Heads of State and Government, Ministers, Ambassadors, distinguished delegates, dear friends. Since this morning, we've heard A number of speeches from this rostrum about the state of the world, and I fear I will not be very original in my description. Every speaker has described the return of imperialism, of arrogance, the return of unrestrained force which knows no rules, a world in which we see power concentrated in the hands of the few, a world in which some believe that they can undermine the international order so as to push their borders outwards, those that believe that people's sovereignty can be toppled over, that they could use that sovereignty, people who believe that they can decide the fate of the planet, whether that be as regards the climate or AI. The question we must answer is very simple. The question is, do we want to live Under this state of affairs, with a return to the law of the jungle, or do we want to live in a civilized international society? Our duty, today more than ever, is to hold firm here at the United Nations in order to make decisions to further our common interests so that people can choose their fate freely their development model, choose their future, to refuse their sovereignty being taken hostage by unjust forces, by fear. Therefore, the very raison d'etre of this organization is to bring together free people on an even footing, an equal footing. It is our charter that prevents the power wielded by some from making decisions for others. This is what compels us to work together to demonstrate our commitment and our capacity to act, and usefully so. You know just how committed France is to the United Nations and its ability to shoulder the responsibilities conferred upon it by the Charter. I wish to reassert our commitment to take action hand in hand with each and every one of you. so as to revive multilateralism and to demonstrate that we are stronger, more effective, more capable of tackling common challenges if we do this together. Today's challenges, future challenges, ones we do not know about yet, challenges we haven't yet tackled. I talked about the climate. It also applies to war and peace, new technologies, and development across all of these areas. Wherever might is right is being imposed, we must defend justice and our common interests. And it is in the interests of each and every one of us as well, because our Charter affords us the protection, the right to live together. Given the sorry state of the world, given what we're seeing today, and that is a growing number of wars we haven't solved, multiplying myriad crises and contemporary challenges which are weighing on new generations in new ways, I believe we are duty bound not to yield. And at the end of the day, the message I wish to convey to you today, as I've been doing over the last nine years, is a message of determination, optimism through action. What I'm trying to tell you is that we will not yield to fatalism, to defeatism, which are very much in vogue. According to this rhetoric, there's not much point coming here to deliver speeches. They say might is right. We can impose a different kind of peace. That is what they say, but we will not give in to that kind of rhetoric, even less so today. We will not yield across five areas. The first is fatalism in the face of war and suffering. We must recommit to finding concrete solutions to building peace. International law never claimed to describe reality. It talked about the limits which sovereign nations themselves set. And in order to ensure when there's a disagreement, force is not the only recourse we have as an option on the table, we must learn the lessons of the 20th century. Those who've forgotten those lessons are committing both a moral error and a political mistake. That is the reality of the situation in the Middle East, in Ukraine, in Africa. War crimes have been industrialized. We've seen the destruction of civilian infrastructure, human rights violations. It's a new era of barbaric acts. The Geneva Conventions offered a protective framework, but it is being dismantled. El-Fasher, Bukavu, Gaza, the list goes on. Together with Jordan and the ICRC, France is going to continue undertaking efforts to ensure the international effort that aims to uphold international humanitarian law, which over 116 states have already rallied behind. will help us to keep our commitments. We must mobilize time and time again to defend international law and international humanitarian law at this time of war. As we've often said, there cannot be peace without justice. And that is why France continues to support politically and operationally the international mechanism aimed at collecting evidence and ensuring justice, in particular to fact-finding missions. We will continue lending our support to the International Court of Justice and supporting the central role it plays. We cannot simply accept this new order of impunity which some are trying to erect. This is why at the Security Council, France supports reforms aimed at bolstering its effectiveness. We must open up to new members, new regions, first and foremost Africa, but In terms of the substance, the Security Council must be able to take action in the face of mass violations of international law. Who can accept a procedural deadlock when we see barbaric acts being committed? The Franco-Mexican initiative on regulating the veto in the case of mass atrocities being committed is needed more than ever, and I'm delighted that it now has the support of 128 member states. The campaign will continue. And we are seeking to secure the commitment of each and every permanent member of the Security Council for this initiative. But it's not enough invoking the law, invoking our values in order to uphold the obligations we all signed up to when we joined the United Nations. We're duty bound to act and France stands ready, working in concert with all those who wish to act in defense of the principles enshrined in the charter, all those who do not wish to remain powerless. The coalition of the willing on Ukraine, together with the UK and Germany, a coalition which brings together everyone who stands ready to guarantee peace and stability in the very heart of Europe, the very place where two world wars began, something no one can ignore. And many in the room today know better than anyone what a return of war to Europe could mean. We will not yield an inch, the coalition of the willing will continue fighting. We also have an independent multinational coalition aimed at restoring the freedom of navigation in the Hormuz Strait. This should not be used for blackmail. It's a cardinal principle of international law, and it is in the interests of all of us for vessels to be able to transit through the strait securely so, and for the energy interests of all of our countries to be secured. The reopening of the Hormuz Strait is a priority. Respect for international law is also a priority. It is in everyone's interests, and France is committed to it. Moving on to Africa, we shoulder a collective responsibility for the crises which are piling up without any answers, without any responses. Peace operations must be more effective. And to this end, they must be endowed with adequate funding and better coordinated with the United States as well as host nations. Back in 2018, I already mentioned the role played by regional organizations and better coordination between these regional bodies and the UN at the Africa forward meeting in Nairobi with over 30 African heads of state and in Addis Ababa, the headquarters of the African Union, together with the UN, we stated clearly that the African Union and regional organizations should be fully equipped to play their role as regards peace and security on the African continent. In Paris in November, we will hold a meeting aimed at replenishing the African Union Peace Fund. This will be on the sidelines of the Paris Peace Forum. I call on all potential funders to make robust and concrete pledges. We will not yield in the face of war. We must recommit and seek solutions that are in keeping with the spirit of the Charter. Second, we must not give in to the permanent temptation to espouse double standards. This is what is dividing our problem, our planet. It is undermining the credibility of our organization and the Charter. How many times have we heard that people's sovereignty has value in Europe, but if we look at the Middle East, at Africa, it is less valuable. No, that is unacceptable. We must defend the same principles across the board. In the spirit of the Charter, support the sovereignty of all peoples. We cannot substitute for their decisions. And every time some states wish to run roughshod over the will of certain peoples to change a system to topple a regime. Every time this resulted in ever greater chaos. No double standards. A life is a life. Peace and security are indivisible. And everyone has a right to them in Ukraine for almost five years now. Russia has been waging a cruel war on civilians. It's been occupying the territory of a sovereign state. France will continue providing unstinting support for the legitimate aspirations of the Ukrainian people to peace, security, and to a future. At the same time, we will spare no effort to ensure that useful negotiations between Russia and Ukraine begin as swiftly as possible. We must defend Ukrainians more than ever as winter is coming. We must defend them On the energy front, we must give them more interceptors. We must protect the civilian population. And this is why we'd like to express our support. A double moratorium. A moratorium on strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure. That's first. And a Black Sea moratorium, which would allow us to release grain shipments Addressing food security concerns, food security being so important for many emerging economies, for many developing nations. This double moratorium is a necessity. Let's put it on the table and let's confront Russia with this reality. In the Middle East, we are also seeking peace and security for all. This is what we defend. respect for sovereignty in Lebanon. Displaced Lebanese people, their villages are being raised in the south. Only a fully sovereign Lebanon will be able to disarm Hezbollah and restore security for all Lebanese and their neighbors. Sovereignty for Lebanon and its people, sovereignty for Palestinians. Their very basic, their most basic rights are once again being violated. One year ago, in this very chamber, several dozen states recognized Palestine. I understand that some are very cynical. You recognized it on paper. Look at the reality of the situation. But what is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza? Some claim that Peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. The spectacle, the spectacle, it is shameful. Shame on all of us. Look, just look at, look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never reactive in the West Bank. What we need is respect for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, their legitimate right to exist. This is a prerequisite for security today and tomorrow for the people of Israel. their security, their very existence to which we're very committed. But all those who claim that Israel's security requires the violation of the sovereignty of all of its neighboring states are making very fateful error. They are weakening Israel's security today and going forward. They are threatening Israel's security in fact. Sovereignty for Syria as well. The revolution should not turn into a disappointment. A few months ago, in Damascus, I lent France's support to building a free Syria, and we must continue these efforts, allowing Syria to fully reassert its sovereignty and unity. France is committed across all of these fronts, just like we're committed with Italy, with the help of Jordan and other friends of Lebanon, We've been committed for 50 years to all Lebanese, so no double standards. Sovereignty for all peoples across the board. My third conviction is that we must not yield to a divided world. Many describe this rift, many talk about this rift between the north and the south. We won't be able to tackle any of the challenges our planet faces if we give in to this rift. And it is fueled by double standards, this rift. However, we need the North and the South to reconcile so that they can tackle climate, health, development challenges. And that's why over the last few years, we've launched many more initiatives. For instance, the COVAX initiative in response to COVID in partnership with the WHO and the African Union. when it came to shoring up economies together with the International Monetary Fund to reform special drawing rights and make progress for African economies. And we held our word, $100 billion in special drawing rights allocated to helping African countries. We must stay the course, ensuring that we remain united. without pitting anyone against anyone else. That is why it's important that the global health infrastructure must remain intact. We will continue reforming that architecture, but we will never weaken the WHO. We must put the finishing touches on the pandemics treaty. And CDC Africa and the WHO should be in a position to combat Ebola ever more effectively. We must be clear-sighted as we reform our official development assistance, ODA. We must ensure that our investments exhibit greater solidarity, that they're more effective. This is what we did with the Paris Pact for People and Planet in 2023. Also at the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, we also agreed to build a new consensus around investment that stands in solidarity with other states. Countries are allocating funds, and yet the needs of the countries of the global south are growing as well. Therefore, desertification, land degradation and drought should not be viewed merely as environmental issues, but should be addressed holistically in connection with food supply and security, water resources, livelihoods, sustainable development and global peace and security. In this spirit, as the presidency of UNCCD COP17, Mongolia has advanced the step action agenda built upon three interconnected flagship initiatives, the Rangelands Flagship Initiative, the Water Land Nexus Initiative, and the Nature-Based Solutions for Sustainable Infrastructure Initiative. Particularly, we regard the Rangelands Flagship Initiative as a landmark global movement that opens a new chapter in the history of rangeland conservation.
