Third, Japan will continue to contribute to the maintenance and development of a free and open international order based on the rule of law. Any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and must never be tolerated anywhere in the world. Russia's aggression against Ukraine is the most obvious example. A permanent member of the Security Council, which is with a special responsibility for international peace and security, has initiated an act of aggression against another country and has vetoed Security Council resolutions concerning its own actions. In this current situation, it must be said that the Security Council is not functioning for international peace. Since the end of Second World War, Japan, as a peace-loving nation, has attached great importance to the rule of law in the settlement of any disputes. This is demonstrated by Japan's consistent support for and its contributions of judges to various international judicial organizations, such as the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court, and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. With this in mind, we established a unit for peace mediation within the government of Japan in March of this year. Japan will play a more proactive role in the peaceful settlement of disputes. Furthermore, the maritime order based on the rule of law is currently being greatly shaken in the Strait of Hormuz. Ensuring free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz for all vessels without additional costs, as has been the case, is extremely important not only for the security of the Middle East, but also for the stability of the global economy as a whole. Similarly, it is essential to ensure stability in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Japan will continue to work closely with relevant countries and the International Maritime Organization, IMO, towards the maintenance of the maritime order in the Middle East.

Madam President, next I would like to set out Japan's efforts and commitments towards the United Nations and multilateralism. Since becoming a member state of the United Nations in 1956, Japan has acted decisively to address global challenges such as eradication of poverty, economic and social development, women's empowerment, climate change, and global health. We have done so through our official development assistance and have deepened our solidarity with the global south. To date, Japan has provided ODA totaling over 670 billion US dollars to developing countries and regions, and has dispatched almost 60,000 Japan Overseas Cooperation Volunteers to 99 countries. Additionally, Japan has been promoting initiatives towards achieving universal health coverage, UHC, across the globe. Since 1993, Japan has co-organized the TCAD together with United Nations. TCAD has served as a platform for reflecting Africa's voice in the Sustainable Development Goals, SDGs, and for Japan to first put forward the concept of VOIP. Africa is endowed with a dynamic young population and possesses enormous economic potential. Japan will continue to promote its diplomacy towards Africa so that Japan and Africa can become more resilient and prosperous together. For example, we will promote industrial development, job creation, and enhanced connectivity in Africa. Furthermore, next year, I will host the Pacific Islands Leaders Meeting, PIM, in Yokohama, Japan, which Japan has convened together with the Pacific Islands region since 1997. Japan aims to further deepen our collaboration with the Pacific Island countries region and promote the stability and prosperity of the region, including addressing common challenges such as maritime security and climate change. Several large scale disasters have occurred and continuously caused extreme damage around the world this year, including in Japan. Natural disasters are becoming more severe and frequent, Japan is striving to become the world's leading nation in disaster risk reduction. To share Japan's expertise and technology in disaster risk reduction and contribute to global efforts in this field, I appointed a new Minister of State for International Disaster Risk Reduction Cooperation in my cabinet reshuffle last week. I myself, in 2015, as Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications, attended the United Nations World Conference on Disaster Reduction, where the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction was adopted. Promoting this framework remains one of our top priorities to this day. It is in Sendai that Japan will host the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in October next year. To protect the lives of present and future generations, all states must take serious action to tackle global warming. I believe that climate action and economic growth can go hand in hand. Japan has been advancing green transformation GX efforts with the goal of achieving net zero by 2050. Such capabilities include establishing the basis for the production and engineering of materials such as green steel, utilizing the world's most efficient gas fire power generation, and popularizing the adoption of energy efficient data centers. harnessing Japan's technological capabilities. We will enhance these efforts with a view to strengthening the resilience of the energy supply demand structure and vigorously advance the policy package for wide energy and resources resilience through green transformation or power GX. Furthermore, Japan will contribute to global climate action, including through GX related efforts such as the Asia Zero Emission Community. that simultaneously achieve decarbonization, energy security, and economic growth. Next year, Japan will host the World Horticultural Exposition 2027 in Yokohama, which is an industrial trade fair showcasing green technologies and approaches to sustainable development. We sincerely hope that many of you will come to join this expo. There are also challenges arising from technological innovation. While advances in AI bring tremendous opportunities for humanity, they also pose challenges, including those related to national security. We also urgently need measures to tackle the spread of information not based on facts, as well as the spread of propaganda. Japan took the initiative to launch the Hiroshima AI Process, establishing the world's first international world's first international principles and code of conduct to govern generative AI. In parallel, Japan has been working with like-minded partners and Global South partners to co-create a safe, secure, and trustworthy AI ecosystem and will enhance cooperation on safety to respond to the risks of highly capable frontier AI. To accelerate these efforts, we intend to host an AI summit in Japan at the earliest opportunity. Madam President, since the end of the Second World War, Japan has built the peace and prosperity it has today through the tireless efforts of our predecessors and the goodwill of a large number of countries. In the course of these efforts, Japan itself has consistently acted in the spirit of multilateralism towards addressing challenges facing the international community. However, these challenges cannot be solved by any single country acting alone. Now more than ever, the flag of the United Nations must be held high, and under that banner, member states must mobilize the collective strength of the membership to elaborate new rules and build a framework for cooperation. I am convinced that the United Nations is the only organization capable of taking the helm on a global scale. To this end as well, reform of the United Nations is essential. The United Nations is a vessel and the responsibility for determining its contents lies with us, namely the member states. Rather than lamenting the institutional fatigue of the United Nations, member states should unite with one heart, vigorously advance reform of the United Nations, and transform the organization into a more resilient and effective United Nations. Let us move forward, building on the achievements of the current Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres. At the same time, the Charter of the United Nations, which is now 81 years old, should also be reviewed. Regarding the so-called enemy states clauses, a United Nations General Assembly resolution was adopted in 2005 to delete references to enemy states from the Charter of the United Nations, expressing the resolve of the heads of state and government of all member states. In accordance with this resolution, these clauses must be deleted. I would like to strongly emphasize this position as Japan takes pride and honor in its significant contributions to the efforts of the United Nations for the last 70 years. Furthermore, as a matter of utmost importance, reform of the Security Council is urgently needed. The current structure of the Security Council, whose mandate is to maintain international peace and security, reflects the international situation as it stood in 1945. We need to transform it without delay into a structure that truly reflects the current realities of the international community. To this end, it is essential to expand the number of both permanent and non-permanent members in order to ensure the legitimacy and representativeness of the Security Council. A majority of member states support the expansion of both categories. Japan is determined to fulfill its solemn responsibility in these UN reforms. Madam President, in the 70 years since we became a UN member state, Japan has consistently contributed to the peace and prosperity of the international community as a peace-loving nation under its exclusively defense-oriented policy. Furthermore, we have worked hand in hand with United Nations on the two indispensable tasks of establishing rules and institutions and providing support on the ground. This policy will remain unchanged in the future. In light of this history, Japan feels a sense of responsibility to safeguard the ideals of the United Nations as our beacon of hope and to carry that light forward into the future. To that end, with its renewed commitment to the United Nations and multilateralism, Japan will continue to steadily take actions. Now, at a time when the world is in turmoil, the United Nations itself must be reborn as a more resilient and effective United Nations and regain the trust of the international community. Together with this more resilient and effective United Nations, Japan is determined to create peace and prosperity by making the Indo-Pacific and the international community more resilient and prosperous. Thank you so very much.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of Japan. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Andy Burnham, Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Madam President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. As the new British Prime Minister, I'm here today to tell you how Britain will deliver leadership in a changing world for the decade that lies ahead, learning from our experience of the last one. It is now 10 years since Brexit. My country has lived through the disruption it brought, and it has given us a unique perspective that I want to share with you today. Britain is back. We are restoring our stability, building a more dynamic economy, a nation that wants to trade with the world and work together to solve the shared problems we face. But we have also learned that we need to adapt to meet the challenge of these times. We need to rebalance power in our country and bring it closer to people. We need to work harder to fight the forces of division and instability which threaten us. Not just through hard power, but through softer, slower means that sow fear and despair. We need to do more to help people with the everyday cost of living and seize the opportunities that give them hope for the future. And we need to embrace the incredible potential of technology to improve people's lives. That's what I want to talk to you about this evening, how the world can come through the turbulence of today to reach towards something better in the decade ahead. Overcoming the forces of division and instability starts with national security. So we will keep investing in our defence, meeting our NATO commitments and strengthening European capabilities. We will be relentless in building up our hard power and deterrence. But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation. Instead, we will be prepared but not panicked, clear-eyed but cool-headed.

and unflinching in defending our people and our allies. True resilience depends on this military strength, but the last 10 years tells us that it is also about something deeper as well. It is about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together. There is no national security without a strong, cohesive society underneath it. That's the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve. But the fact is, it has been under attack. In recent years, we have seen industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies. Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears. They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives, And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election. We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events. The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive, but it is what they do. The Kremlin spends around 1.3 billion pounds each year on manipulating information. We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division, and sowing despair. On top of that, we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions, and we know that AI will multiply the threat. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade, we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more. We are going to face the new decade in a different way, with our eyes wide open. We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law, and we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience Because faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home. If you're struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving, or if you're a young person not in employment, education or training, you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence. So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. So we will work to make life more affordable for people. That will be at the heart of a new 10-year plan for Britain that we will bring forward later in the year. And we will put in place the architecture to stem this poisonous tide. Today, I am asking our security chiefs in the UK to begin work on a new National Centre for Information Defence. to detect, attribute, and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks, to support and defend our democracy. I know this is a shared challenge, so we are going to use our experience in the UK and the fact that we have already been through this shock, starting 10 years ago, to help other countries. We have already supported Moldova to protect its elections from Russian interference. As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues, some for the first time. So we're ready to share our understanding of how these actors work and how we can respond, because this is a vital task for our collective security and resilience. To overcome division and instability, we must also find new ways to bring countries together. We know that we are at our strongest when we unite with others, when we reach across borders to solve shared problems. Standing here today, I am reminded of the huge human progress that this organization has led, like the eradication of smallpox or the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. That is the kind of promise and hope that led Britain to host the very first meeting of this General Assembly in London, and led to the world to create this institution, these United Nations, our United Nations. That is the level of ambition that we need now to renew the UN for our times, to tackle challenges like improving global health and preventing future pandemics, to end the wars that are causing so much suffering and instability, including the terrible conflict in Sudan, and to tackle climate change. The climate crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world, as this summer of extreme heat, wildfires, and floods has proved beyond doubt. Britain will continue to lead with others to fight this threat, to protect our children and grandchildren, to protect the natural world, and also to seize the benefits for jobs, growth, and reindustrialization that the clean energy transition can bring. So we must raise our sights. And I believe the United Kingdom has a unique position as an honest broker to help drive this forward. We are America's closest ally. We have deep ties with our friends in the European Union and seek to deepen them further. We work with China and emerging powers like India and Brazil. We sit on the UN Security Council, in the Commonwealth, in the CPTPP. In a divided world, we have the ability to bring people together And we will. We are going to step into that role and we are going to start with one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age, frontier AI. AI brings together so many of the most pressing issues before us. It is already speeding up cancer diagnosis in the UK, but AI has the potential to go further, not just to help prevent and treat cancer, but to help cure it. AI will also be the key to economic growth, the route to transforming education, and it will be a vital tool to keep us safe. I am announcing today that we are developing a new AI defense partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure. But we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, a multiplier of risk. We've all heard the warnings, which we must heed. I know how worried people are, so we have to rise to this moment. Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance. They must be taken by elected governments who serve working people. and we need to give people the support they need through this change, ensuring that it becomes an engine for reindustrialisation and opportunity as well. There is a lesson from the first industrial revolution, which started in northern England two centuries ago. It was a time of incredible technological progress, but for workers, the disruption brought huge suffering and exploitation. Things got a lot worse before they got better. So this time, we need to get it right. I believe we're more than equal to the task. The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world. And when it comes to guarding against the risks, we have our world-leading AI Security Institute, working hand in glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety. But we need to go further. Building on the meeting convened by His Majesty King Charles last week, I can announce today that I am going to put AI at the heart of the UK's G20 presidency next year. I look back at how we responded to the financial crisis back in 2008. We moved quickly in the G20 and smaller groups to deliver an urgent, practical response. We came together to agree principles which everyone implemented at home in a way that was right for them, and it worked. That is the kind of approach we need now. So we will bring the right people together on the key issues, delivering on the potential of AI for good and dealing with the risks. And we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe. This will bring together welcome initiatives from others, like that proposed by Norway this week. As His Majesty said, the task before us is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity. And I want to reassure the British people that ultimately, we will do whatever is necessary to protect them, including bringing forward new laws if that is what is needed. They need to know that we will protect their interests, and we will. But on its own, that's not enough, is it? In this dangerous, turbulent age, it is more important than ever that we give people the power to build their own resilience and do more for themselves. and give them the platform to stand up for what they believe in. I am working to rebalance power across all regions of the UK. And as part of that, I have set up a second Downing Street office in Manchester. We call it Number 10 North. Outside that office stands a statue of Abraham Lincoln. It marks the personal connection he made with Manchester and the bond between our two nations. a bond which he described in a letter to the working people of the city as perpetual. This was not due to some military or material support. There was no quid pro quo. It was because Manchester's humble mill workers took a principled stand. During the American Civil War in 1862, despite the hardships it brought them, they refused to touch raw cotton that had been picked by slaves. in 1862. People with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world. The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people. And whatever distorted view social media offers today, the world is still full of good and decent people all over the world who are ready to stand up for what is right. I see that shining through all the time. Nothing brings the British people together across age, race and class more than their hatred of injustice, the misuse of power against the powerless. We will always stand for the underdog against the bully. That's why we are so united behind Ukraine. And let me say, we salute the Ukrainian people. They are showing depths of resilience and courage. That is an inspiration to the whole world. I was in Kyiv last month, and it gave me a glimpse of life under Russian attack. I went to a bustling market, just a normal scene from any European city. The traders singing the praises of their products, pushing into my hands peaches and plums from Odessa. But their stalls were out on the street because the market hall had been destroyed. In the background, there were burned out cars. Behind us, a building that had taken a direct hit just a few weeks before. I met people riding the metro home from work, people just getting on with their lives. But at night, those same metro stations doubling as shelters for thousands of people, from the elderly to little kids, some who have known nothing but war. People told me about the freezing conditions in the stations last winter, when temperatures dropped below minus 20 degrees outside. Meanwhile, Russia was targeting their energy infrastructure, trying to make them suffer even more. We can't let them do that again this winter. So we're working to help Ukraine protect their skies and civilians. We're leading the charge in raising the cost for Russia of continuing this senseless and illegal war. The Graham bill, which President Trump signed last week, will make a huge difference to that effort. And we will support Ukraine to repair and protect the heat and power plants that Kyiv will depend upon this winter. It is right that we provide that support. But we should call Russia out this time and every time. Everyone in this room knows that strikes on civilian infrastructure are explicitly forbidden by international law. Yet we stand here in the UN announcing funding to mitigate the effects of these war crimes, which we reliably expect to be perpetrated yet again by a permanent member of the Security Council. It must end. Russia could choose a different course tomorrow, accept a ceasefire, come to the negotiating table. I urge them to do so. But until then, we will stand with Ukraine, stronger than ever, for as long as it takes. This is about upholding the UN Charter and the rule of law. We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law, not just from Russia, but from others too, including where they threaten the rights of British territories, to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands. That's why we're also working with France and other partners to support freedom of navigation in the Gulf. And it's why I have acted on the Middle East. Just eight weeks into becoming Prime Minister, working with my Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, I comprehensively reset our position. And we built an international coalition of countries to come with us. The terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 was utterly horrific. I have condemned it in the strongest possible terms. We continue to condemn Hamas, and we stand with Israel in the face of the ongoing threats, including from Iran, against Israel and Jewish people around the world. But this does not justify the Israeli Government's actions in Gaza or the West Bank. Far too many people have died, including so many children. Far too little aid is getting in. And it has gone on for far too long. We will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution, the best hope for peace and stability for both nations, comes under attack. Last month, Israel issued tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement, which would drive a wedge through the West Bank and threaten to put a viable Palestinian state beyond reach. It cannot be allowed to happen. So we have acted by banning trade in goods with illegal settlements, recognising that the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful, and sanctioning those taking part in the construction of illegal settlements. We want to see the suffering and death finally come to an end. We want to see Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security. And we will do all we can to keep the hope of that possibility alive. And look, we live in an age of low trust in politics. If we were to continue to talk about the two-state solution, but fail to back those words with deeds, that trust will fall even lower and our enemies will seek to exploit the alienation that follows from that. We won't let it happen. So, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this is the kind of leadership Britain is here to bring. We need to recommit together to make the decade ahead of us better than the last. My message to our partners around the world is this: you can count on us. Count on us to stand up for those long-standing British values of fairness and justice, our shared values, and for the UN Charter. Count on us to fight racism, discrimination and the abuse of power wherever we see it, just as those Manchester cotton workers did in the 19th century, and the country did in the fight against fascism in the 20th century. Count on us to bring people together, not to point towards old problems, but to work towards new solutions for the 21st century. Count on us to meet fear and division with unity and hope. Thank you very much indeed.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency, Andriy Plenkovic, Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia. I request protocol to escort his Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Good evening, Madam Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. We come to this Assembly from countries that differ in size, population and power. Yet here, precisely because of that, every country has its unique experience to share, responsibilities to assume, and a contribution to make. Croatia brings the experience of a nation that within one generation endured aggression and occupation, defended its freedom, and rebuilt itself. It joined the UN, NATO, and the EU, and developed a flourishing democracy and a growing economy. Our path and our transition were neither straight or easy, but we made it. Over the past decade as Prime Minister, I have seen Croatia translate those experiences into progress at home and more responsibility abroad. They have reinforced three convictions that speak directly to the theme of this session. First, rules are our common compass. Second, Transformation help us build resilience. Third, trust is earned only through delivery. Ladies and gentlemen, we support rule-based multilateralism as the pinnacle of human cooperation, not because we are naive, but because we have seen and experienced the alternative. For smaller and medium-sized states, international law is not an abstraction. It is the line between order and tyranny, between sovereign equality and the rule of force. The rule of force, such as witnessed by Croatia during the brutal aggression and occupation of more than one quarter of our territory in the 90s, in the war which claimed nearly 20,000 lives, and after which, more than three decades later, Croatia continues to search for 1,725 missing persons, a poignant example that the consequences of war do not end when the weapons fall silent. Instead, peace requires courage, credible institutions, and rules that apply equally to everyone. Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine is a direct assault on those rules. Croatia will continue to support Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, and a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace based on the UN Charter. Peace cannot reward conquest, and recovery cannot be separated from justice. The same compass must guide us in the Middle East. Protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, respect for international law, and a credible political horizon are essential to breaking the cycle of violence. Croatia supports a negotiated two-state solution in which Israelis and Palestinians will live in peace and security. From Sudan and Myanmar to the Sahel and the Great Lakes region, civilians bear the highest cost when rules are ignored and diplomacy fails. And no crisis remains local for long. War disrupts food and energy supplies, while insecurity from the Strait of Hormuz to the Black Sea affects shipping, prices and livelihoods across continents. This is why, as a government, we are dealing with the consequences of energy price pressures by passing degrees to protect Croatian citizens and economy from energy shocks created far away from our shores. As distant as they may seem, these shocks are real, as they ripple into domestic inflationary pressures, affecting everything from wages and pensions to food prices and basic services. This is why freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the strict implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea matter to everyone. For us, freedom of navigation and maritime security are both a national interest and a global responsibility. Common rules do not hold us back. They provide the stability and predictability necessary for countries to advance their ambitions. The world is being transformed by technology, climate change, demographic pressures, illegal migration, and geopolitical rivalry. Our responsibility is to govern them so that change expands human freedom and security instead of weakening them. The United Nations must begin with its own transformation. Croatia supports a UN that is more effective, accountable and financially sustainable, and stronger across all three pillars: peace and security, sustainable development and, of course, human rights. Reform must also produce a more representative and effective Security Council. When the Council is blocked, the General Assembly can and must act, but it cannot replace the Council's primary responsibility under the Charter. This makes the selection of the next Secretary-General all the more relevant. I thank, therefore, Secretary-General Guterres for his work over the last decade. The United Nations needs leadership capable of bringing Member States together defending the Charter and turning reform into measurable results. No country alone can successfully respond to the global transformations we witness today. Artificial intelligence can accelerate development, but its use must remain consistent with legal frameworks, human dignity and democratic accountability. Renewed nuclear rhetoric makes a firm commitment to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons more important than ever. Climate action should be used to strengthen energy security and social cohesion. Our experience shows that the green transition should not be ideological. It can endure only when it is technologically realistic, socially fair, compatible with secure and affordable energy, and supportive of overall development. For Europe, which imports most of the energy it consumes, the case for producing more renewable energy at home now reaches far beyond climate policy. It is a strategic necessity. It strengthens Europe's sovereignty and capacity to act, reduces external dependence, creates economic opportunity, and makes our societies more resilient. The same principle applies to illegal migration, which has caused mistrust in Europe and altered the political landscape in many countries. This situation is unacceptable and it cannot continue. The rule of law must be upheld and legal procedures must be followed. Our primary responsibility is to our citizens and it starts at our borders. We are not allowing uncontrolled migration and we are fighting the criminal networks that facilitate it. As an EU external border country, Croatia carries an additional responsibility and we will fulfill it with determination. Transformation is equally important in our own neighborhood. Southeast Europe remains the unfinished part of the European project. Croatia will continue to support merit-based EU enlargement. EU membership can turn borders of division into lines of cooperation, and reforms on paper into stronger institutions and better living standards. But European transformation requires honesty about the past. Reconciliation becomes possible when responsibility for the crimes of the past is acknowledged and their glorification rejected. That standard allows no national exceptions. That means respect for victims and clear rejection of historical revisionism, not the glorification of war criminals. Radko Mladic was a convicted war criminal responsible for the Srebrenica genocide, the first genocide in Europe since the Holocaust. While his criminal record reached its nefarious culmination in Srebrenica, his trail of war crimes stretches further back to the shelling of Croatian cities, the murder of civilians, the mining of dams, and the destruction of cultural heritage and industrial facilities. The military and official honours accorded to Mladic in Serbia were an affront to his victims and to the judgements of international courts. The participation of state representatives in the public claim that accompanied the ceremony is totally incompatible with the values of a union Serbia seeks to join. The same commitment to equality and reform should guide Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a signatory to the Dayton Peace Accords and a neighbor and a friend of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia is one of the strongest advocates of its European future. The Dayton Peace Accords ended the war and established the constitutional framework for Bosnia and Herzegovina, one state, two entities, and three constituent peoples: Croats, Bosniaks, and Serbs. That balance is the foundation on which peace was built. Yet the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina are still being denied legitimate representation, including in the presidency of the country. That is unjust. destabilizing and contrary to the spirit of Dayton. The solution is neither division nor domination. It is carefully designed electoral reform that protects every citizen while ensuring that a basic principle of legitimate political representation of the constituent peoples is restored. Croatia will not tire of explaining why this reform is crucial for the entire country to reach its full potential. and we will not tire of opposing those political forces whose short-sighted pursuit of political gains jeopardizes equality of constituent peoples and the long-term prosperity. Our own history confirms that transformation succeeds when it is rooted in inclusion, responsibility, and reform. Over the past decade, Croatia has doubled the size of its economy in nominal terms. while reducing its public debt to GDP ratio by 30 percentage points from its pandemic peak. Six consecutive sovereign credit rating upgrades have brought us into the A category. We have tripled our defense budget with approximately one-third of that spending allocated to military modernization. In a changed security environment, we are strengthening our security and ensuring we are better equipped to support international stabilization missions abroad. Reforms we are pursuing domestically are increasing our overall resilience and giving us increased capacity to engage in a world which is rapidly changing. Ladies and gentlemen, the international system stutters when the distance between declaration and delivery becomes too wide. Trust returns when cooperation produces real, measurable results. It returns when a child is in school, a community is protected from violence, a mine is removed from a field, or food reaches family. And it returns when institutions prevent conflict before it even begins. Last year alone, the world's official development assistance was reduced by almost 25%. This drop is the largest annual contraction on record for international aid. Refusing to spiral into negative trends, Croatia is contributing more, not less. Between 2016 and 24, our official development assistance increased fivefold, while our humanitarian assistance grew more than 21 fold. With our UN partners, we are translating our commitment and funds into action. We support girls education in Kenya, provide humanitarian assistance in Gaza, and assist Syrian refugee children. We also advance mine action in Ukraine, drawing on Croatia's own post-war experience, and protect women and girls from digital violence. This practical, inclusive and human-centred approach is also what Croatia brings to ECOSOC. If elected to the presidency of ECOSOC for the 27-28 cycle, Croatia will work to strengthen coordination and accountability. As 2030 approaches, accelerating implementation of the Sustainable Goals continues to be a central priority. Croatia persistently ranks among the world's 15 highest performing countries in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals. Our experience is not a universal prescription, but evidence that national reform and international responsibility can and do advance together. It is this credibility that is in the foundation of trust in multilateralism that we wish to see rebuilt. Credibility which is strongest when every country, regardless of its size, wealth, or power, has a meaningful voice. The answer is therefore not less multilateralism that delivers, it is multilateralism that must deliver. It is this approach that Croatia would bring to the Security Council if elected to serve in 2030-31. Excellencies, Croatia's modern journey began in war, but war did not define its destination. Our experience has shaped the way we understand international cooperation and the responsibilities that come with it. Rules gave us a compass when force sought to erase our borders. Reform gave us a bridge from vulnerability to resilience and from post-war recovery to membership in the EU, the euro area and Schengen. Delivery turned those ambitions into institutions, security and better lives for our citizens and gave us the capacity to contribute beyond our borders. That is the experience Croatia brings to the United Nations. Not a claim to perfection, but the perspective of a country that has traveled a difficult road and learned from it. The United Nations remains indispensable because no country can navigate today's storms alone. Let us therefore rebuild trust by defending our common compass and managing change so that it strengthens human dignity. Let us ensure that our commitment reach the people for whom they were made. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia. I now give the floor to his Excellency Maxime Prevost, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, European Affairs and Development Cooperation of Belgium.

Madam Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Maurice Maeterlinck, born in Ghent and awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1911, wrote a strange, almost unsettling play entitled The Blind. 12 people find themselves in a forest on an island. The guide who led them there is sitting among them. He is dead, but they don't know it yet. They are waiting for him to return. They hear the wind, the sea, the voices around them. They know they are not alone, yet they can barely tell where the others are. At one point, one of the characters says, "Years and years we have been together, and we have never seen each other. That line comes back to me when I look at our world. We, too, are together. We meet constantly. We exchange statements, messages, and positions. At times, we spend hours around the same tables. And yet, being in the same room doesn't mean that we understand one another. Do we still take the time to hear what others are telling us, to understand what they fear, what they need, and what the world looks like from where they stand? That, to me, is where diplomacy begins. Not when we agree, but when we no longer do. Diplomacy is not erasing disagreements, nor about abandoning our principles to secure consensus at any costs. It is about continuing to speak, continuing to listen, and finding ways to manage our differences without allowing them to lead to a breakdown in relations or to confrontation. In the play, one of the characters says something very simple. Let us try to draw a little closer. Martin Luther King wrote those words more than a century ago. Yet, they feel entirely relevant today. Drawing closer doesn't mean thinking alike. It means refusing to let distance turn into indifference. then mistrust, until eventually we stop speaking altogether. That risk is real today. It is one of the paradoxes of our time. We have never been more connected, yet we do not necessarily understand one another any better. Our economies, societies, and technologies has become deeply interdependent, even as the temptation to turn inward returns with force. In other words, we depend on one another more than ever, at the very moment when we are sometimes tempted to believe that we can do without one another. The more interdependent we become, the more we need common rules, not to erase our differences, not to impose a single vision of the world, but to ensure that we can manage our disagreements without allowing the law of the strongest to become the only law that matters. In the play, The Blind, the characters have lost the person who was meant to show them the way. We are not in the same position. No one will come and decide for us which direction to take. But that doesn't mean we can move forward without bearings. Faced with wars, humanitarian crisis, climate disruption, pandemics and technological upheaval. The question is ultimately quite simple. Do we still have a common compass? For Belgium, the answer is yes. That compass is the Charter of the United Nations. It is international law. But the rule has value only if it continues to apply when respecting it becomes difficult. It is precisely when the law runs counter to a state's immediate interest that we discover whether it truly matters. When a signature loses its value the moment it becomes binding, When a treaty holds only for as long as it suits the party that signed it, it is not merely a legal text that is weakened. It is trust in a promise made. And with it, the security of all those who believed they could rely on that promise. That is why Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine concerns far more than two states. When a border can be changed by force, every border becomes less secure. No one in this room needs reminding that international politics is shaped by power and by interest. The Charter doesn't wish those realities away. It draws a line around what power may be alone to do. And for Belgium, ladies and gentlemen, that line matters in very practical terms. We are an open economy, with an economy tied to the world and a security bound up with that of our partners. We depend on states keeping their word, on agreements surviving changes in the balance of power, and on borders not being redrawn at gunpoint. International law reflects our values, certainly. It also protects our interests. This is why Belgium stands firmly with Ukraine. Any lasting peace must be grounded in the Charter of the United Nations and in respect for Ukraine's sovereignty, political independence, and territorial integrity. But we cannot uphold these principles on my continent alone, in Europe, and treat them as optional elsewhere. Sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the right of peoples to determine their own future do not change meaning when we cross the borders of a continent. The same standard must guide us when it comes to international humanitarian law. Its rules do not apply only when they suit us. They exist precisely for the moment when respecting them becomes difficult. In the state of Palestine, in Sudan, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, and so many other places, scared by war or armed violence, the circumstances differ, but no human life is worth less than another. Civilians remain civilians. They must be protected. Humanitarian aid must be allowed to reach them everywhere. And this year again, hundreds of millions of people need humanitarian assistance while the resources available to help them are shrinking. When funding runs out, what do we tell the mother who asks war for hours to reach a clinic with a sick child that the doors are closed? What do we tell to a family waiting for food that there will be no delivery tomorrow? We cannot ask humanitarian workers to give those answers because we have chosen to cut their funding. This is not the time to treat humanitarian aid as an optional expertise and expense. It is neither a reward nor a bargaining chip. An hungry child is not responsible for the position taken by his government. That child has the right to eat, the right to receive care, and the right to be protected. That is why I urge every one of us not to cut humanitarian funding. International law does more than contain violence. It also enables trade, exchange, and movement. That brings me to a freedom that may at first sound rather technical, freedom of navigation. For my country, Belgium, it is anything but technical. As early as the 19th century, the port of Antwerp had immense potential. But ships sailing up the River Scheldt had to pay a toll. In 1863, an international agreement abolished that toll once and for all. The abolition was to apply to all flags, all of them. An international route has real value only if it remains open. Passage cannot depend each time on a fresh contest of power. That is precisely what freedom of navigation represents today. It is not merely the abstract right of a ship to travel from a point to another. It allows economies that may share neither the same interests nor the same alliances to remain connected. It allows a landlocked state to take part in global trade. It allows grain, medicines, gas, and industrial components to cross several maritime areas without the passage having to be negotiated at every stage. That seems perfectly normal while everything is working. But it takes only one route closing for us to remember how much it matters. Think of the Strait of Hormuz, the Sable Mandate Strait at the entrance of the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, the Bosporus, the Strait of Malacca, or the Panama Canal. More than 80% of global merchandise trade by volume is carried by sea. When a ship is attacked, when a strait becomes dangerous, or when a carrier has to sail around an entire region, the effects are felt thousands of kilometers away. In our ports, of course, but also in the price of energy, fertilizer, and food. The price of a tank of fuel the price of a loaf of bread, even having a bread. And very often, the countries with the least economic room to maneuver bear the greatest burden in proportional terms. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea confers rights, but it also imposes obligations. the safety of navigation, the protection of the marine environment, and respect for the rights of coastal states. A smaller navy doesn't mean fewer rights, nor does a larger one confer the right to impose its will. No country should have to surrender the rights the law gives simply because another can send more ships. That is why maritime disputes must be settled by law, not by intimidation. And that is why freedom of navigation depends on common rules, so that every country can exercise its rights. while respecting those of others. But keeping our sea routes open also means keeping them safe all the way into our ports. The International Ship and Port Facility Security Code, the famous ISPS Code, offers a very concrete example of what multilateralism can achieve when it works. Piracy, terrorism and crime are scoundrels that we must fight together. And that code must be strengthened. Belgium understands its importance. Freedom and security are not opposing ideas. Security is a condition of freedom. I dwell on freedom of navigation because it illustrates something larger. Sovereignty doesn't require isolation. We can defend our interests while accepting that others have rights too. And when rules are clear and predictable enough, a space of competition can still remain a space of cooperation. The ocean, moreover, are far more than the highways of our trades. They feed populations, regulate our climates, and absorb much of the excess heat caused by global warming. For many small island states, Rising sea levels affect the land on which the citizens live, the economy, some cases, the culture, and the very ability to remain where the families have lived for generations. The freedom to use the ocean therefore comes with a responsibility to preserve it. And on this point, Allow me to be optimistic. The BBNJ agreements enter into force this year after almost 20 years of negotiations. Almost 20 years. Measured against a political cycle, this is close to an eternity. Measured against the building of international law, it is sometimes the time needed to reach a compromise strong enough to last. The agreement proves that even today, we continue to build international law rather than dismantle it. And Belgium has invested greatly in this process. It helped launch the Blue Leaders, a coalition of countries working to protect at least 30% of the ocean by 2030 and secure an ambitious ICS treaty. The BBNJ agreements now gives us an essential tool to advance towards that protection goal. But 20 years of negotiations must not be followed by years of waiting. It is in that spirit that Belgium is offering to host the treaty's future secretariat in Brussels. We are ready to enable it to work from day one. It will be able to draw on our scientific expertise and on a community that brings together international organizations, embassies, and civil society. So that we have agreed together becomes real protection at sea. Beneath those same oceans run other vital routes. The cables that connect the continents and carry much of our digital communications and energy. Here too, our interdependence is plain to see. A break, an act of sabotage, or an attack can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. Protecting those connections is essential. But our responsibility in the digital world doesn't end with infrastructure. Artificial intelligence already confronts us with another question. How can we make full use of the possibilities created by innovation without allowing technology to move faster than our ability to protect people? I'm thinking in particular of children who are growing up in a world where AI can open extraordinary possibilities but also creates new vulnerabilities. We must neither hold back innovation out of fear, nor assume that it will regulate itself. As AI sees in the digital world, freedom needs rules if it is to remain freedom. We cannot speak about interdependence without speaking about migration. People have always moved, and they will continue to do so. And governments have a duty to manage that movement and to ensure that migration takes place safely, regularly, and in accordance with the law. Order is itself a matter of human rights. When migration is left in the hands of smugglers and traffickers, people are exploited, placed in danger, and sometimes lost at sea. But the way in which governments maintain order matters just as much. States have both the right and the responsibility to manage the borders. They must do so in full respect of international law and fundamental rights. A person's legal status may change. Their human dignity doesn't. Every person counts. That is why countries of origin, transit, and destination must work together.

Safe, orderly and regular migration and respect for human rights are not competing ambitions. They must go hand in hand. And we can either manage our interdependence or be at its mercy. Health crises have taught us the same lesson. Outbreaks do not recognize borders. Cooperation is a necessity. Those who refuse to cooperate weaken themselves. But if our commitments are to hold, we also need institutions capable of upholding them. The law needs guardians. And this year, we mark the 18th anniversary of the International Court of Justice. It settles legal disputes submitted to it by states peacefully and in accordance with international law. The International Criminal Court has a different mandate to fight impunity by prosecuting and trying individuals accused of the gravest international crimes. Their mandates differ. Their independence must be defended equally. Both courts rest on the same idea: power cannot be its own judge. That remains true even when we dislike their rulings or proceedings. When judges or staff members of an international court face sanctions or pressure for carrying out their mandates, Belgium will always stand with them to protect them. But the promise of the law doesn't end in courtrooms or in relations between states. It concerns people. human rights, the right to think and speak freely, freedom of conscience and religion, and the freedom not to believe. It concerns the ability of every woman to decide the course of her own life and take an equal place in society. This ability to love the person we love without fear of prison, of violence, of persecution. These freedoms belong to no single continent. They rest on an elementary conviction. A person's dignity doesn't depend on their sex, their origin, their sexual orientation, or what a government thinks of them. Our societies are different, ladies and gentlemen. They will remain so. Human dignity doesn't require us to be alike in order to be equal. That conviction also guides our diplomacy. Dialogue is not approval. Dialogue is not the opposite of resolve. Diplomacy requires both. It also requires institutions capable of functioning. Defending the United Nations doesn't mean pretending that everything within it works well. The UN80 process is necessary. But there is a difference between reforming an organization and weakening it. We cannot ask more of it, steadily strip away its resources, and then express surprise when it's not effective enough. Reform must preserve what gives the organization its purpose, peace and security. human rights and development. It must also ensure better representation for every region of the world. And more than 80 years ago, ladies and gentlemen, Paul-Henri Spaak led the Belgian delegation to the San Francisco Conference that gave birth to the United Nations. A few months later, he became the first President of this General Assembly. Belgium was emerging from war and occupation. That is precisely why multilateralism seemed the obvious choice to us. We are not here to preserve an institution for its own sake. We are here to preserve what it must make possible. peace and security, human rights, and prosperity for all. So, ladies and gentlemen, before we were presidents, ministers, ambassadors, or diplomats, we were all children. And despite all that sets them apart, the people we represent often want remarkably simple things. to come home in the evening, to watch their children grow up and send them to school without fear, to work, to love the person they love, to make plans for next year, not to live with the thought that war, hunger, disease, or violence could make everything disappear overnight. That is the most concrete definition of peace, being able to live your life without constantly fearing that you will lose it. We can build peace and we can damage it. We can pass it on or leave the next generation with the task of starting all over again. At the beginning of this speech, I spoke of Maurice Maeterlinck's play, The Blind. Its characters were waiting for someone to show them the way. We cannot simply wait. No one will come and decide for us what kind of world we want to live in. But we are not without bearings. We have international law. We have dialogue. And above all, we have a responsibility to use them both. A compass cannot prevent a storm. It helps us hold our course when the storm comes. I thank you.

Thank the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, European Affairs and Development Cooperation of Belgium. I now give the floor to his excellency, Nasser Burita, Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation, and Moroccans Abroad of Morocco.

Your Excellency, President of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I extend my sincere congratulations on behalf of the delegation of the Kingdom of Morocco to His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the General Assembly at its 81st session, and I wish him every success in his lofty mission. I also commend the tireless efforts of Secretary-General Antonio Guterres since he assumed the leadership of our Organization. Amid the major divisions the world has experienced over the past decade, he has emerged as a voice of wisdom, consensus and pragmatism, defending tirelessly and courageously the United Nations system and international law as the two fundamental pillars for the maintenance of international peace and security. Mr. Guterres has remained a symbol of multilateral diplomacy and of international cooperation in overcoming the turmoil and obstacles facing our world today. Mr. President, the most apt description of our international reality is the one expressed by His Majesty King Mohammed VI. 6. May God assist him when His Majesty said, and I quote, "The world is changing at an unprecedented pace, and certainties are steadily receding. This has led to a blurring of standards and concepts. Alliances have become open to question. International law is frequently violated, and its capacity to regulate international relations faces numerous challenges." End of quote from His Majesty the King. We are therefore facing a world whose fundamental features are the following. First, the escalation of acute and diverse international crises, military, economic, energy related and environmental. Second, the spread of confrontational tendencies as a key determinant of relations between states. Third, The difficulty of predicting the outcome of crises. We know when they begin, but not when they will end. Fourth, the diminishing capacity of existing regulatory structures to play the role in preventing and managing crises. In this complex international context, Mr. President, I wish to focus on three areas to which the international community must accord priority. First, confronting non-state armed groups as a threat to international security and stability. Second, addressing climate change and its effects. Third, tackling regional challenges, particularly in the Middle East and Africa. The role of non-state armed groups. that threaten the security and stability of states has grown considerably. Indeed, they now seek to control maritime corridors and straits and to threaten freedom of navigation. They also target facilities in a number of countries. At the global level, more than 200 million people live in areas under the control of armed groups or in contested areas. Moreover, more than 130 non-state armed groups have been identified as legally classified parties to armed conflicts. These figures clearly reflect the scale of the spread and proliferation of these groups in a world that, over the past two decades, has become less secure and less stable. Further, the close links between these armed groups and separatist militias on the one hand, and terrorist organizations and criminal networks, as well as mercenary elements on the other hand, are evident to all. It is therefore a mistake to believe that some of these groups are peaceful or constructive, or that they can engage in the settlement of conflicts. All these groups use violence to impose a fait accompli and to serve the agenda of those who control them. They must therefore be dealt with firmly, and responsibility must be assigned to the states that sponsor, harbor, finance and arm them. and provide them with safe haven and support. The responsibility of these sponsoring states is not merely political, it is also legal, moral, and historical. These groups and their sponsors alike cannot be allowed to become a means of evading responsibility or a tool for carrying out what states cannot do directly. Hence, Deterrent sanctions must be imposed on these groups and their sponsors. All those who provide them with support, financing, or arms must be held accountable. Mr. President, there can be no way to sustain peace and development without effectively addressing the challenge of climate change, which is no longer a future threat. It is already affecting water and food security. As well as the stability of territories, economies and the living conditions of populations. Despite its limited contribution to greenhouse gas emissions, Morocco remains among the countries most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change accordingly. In line with the vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him, the Kingdom has adopted a proactive policy based on the continued construction of dams, the interconnection of water basins, sea water desalination, the reuse of treated wastewater, and the rationalization of water resource management, particularly in the agricultural sector. This national effort forms part of an international commitment to climate action. On that basis, the Kingdom has set for the period 2026-2035 a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by up to 53% by 2035, while placing adaptation and the strengthening of territorial resilience at the top of its priorities. This effort has extended to the African continent, which suffers from the devastating effects of climate change. The Royal Initiative to establish three African Climate Commissions for the Congo Basin, the Sahel region, and the African Island States has generated promising momentum to strengthen African climate action and coordination among the states of the continent in addressing these challenges. However, addressing climate change cannot rely on national effort alone. It requires the provision of affordable and accessible financing, technology transfer, and genuine international solidarity, enabling developing countries to fulfill their responsibilities towards present and future generations alike. Mr. President, Madam President, The Palestinian question remains a constant priority in the foreign policy of the Kingdom of Morocco, based on its belief in the justice of this, that this is a just cause and it's central to achieving peace and stability in the Middle East region. Building on this conviction, the Kingdom of Morocco, under the leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, believes that the establishment of a lasting peace in the Middle East depends on the establishment of an independent, sovereign, and viable Palestinian state on the borders of the 4th of June 1967, with East Jerusalem as its capital, living side by side with the State of Israel in peace and security. In the face of the tragedy that the brotherly Palestinian people continue to endure, the Kingdom renews its call for respect for the ceasefire in Gaza and for the entry of humanitarian assistance into the Strip in sufficient quantities without impediment or interruption. At the same time, Morocco stresses the need to support the Palestinian Authority, particularly in the financial, technical, structural, humanitarian, and training fields, and to accompany the reforms it is undertaking within its various institutions. Morocco also renews its support for the pivotal role of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East, UNRWA. In keeping with its approach of supporting initiatives aimed at achieving peace in the Middle East, Morocco has decided to participate in the International Stabilization Force in Gaza and to contribute through humanitarian and security initiatives to establishing a climate of peace and security in the region by contributing to the training of the Palestinian police. deploying high-ranking military officers to the internal security forces, and setting up a military field hospital, in addition to its readiness to lead a program to counter extremism. Developments in the West Bank are deeply alarming. including the adoption of certain laws that affect the legal status of the Palestinian territory and pave the way for the seizure for the purpose of settlement expansion, as well as the systematic violence perpetrated by Israeli settlers against Palestinian citizens. All these measures point in one direction: the displacement of the population, and the undermining of the material basis for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state. With regard to the city of Jerusalem, Morocco expresses its deep concern about unilateral Israeli measures and the repeated violations of the sanctity of Al-Aqsa Mosque, which constitutes serious transgressions that contribute to fueling the discourse of extremism and hatred at the expense of the voice of wisdom and moderation. As the chair of Al-Quds Committee, His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him, continues his work to preserve the historical, cultural, and spiritual identity of the Holy City and its legal status, as well as to improve the living conditions of the Maghdisi inhabitants, combining political and diplomatic action with programs implemented on the ground by Bayt Mal Al-Quds Al-Sharif Agency, the executive arm of Al-Quds Committee. Mr. President, despite its significant human, natural and civilizational assets, the African continent faces a gap between the scale of the commitments announced for its benefit by the international community and the value of what has actually been achieved on the ground. Contrary to the stereotypical image held by some, Africa is not a continent of conflicts and a hotbed of problems, rather it is a land of opportunity and potential, capable of devising solutions and putting forward initiatives. That is the idea summed up by His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him, in his eloquent words: "Africa must trust Africa", the enlightened royal vision for Africa, which has materialized through a significant number of projects. stems from a firm conviction that the continent has attained a level of maturity that qualifies it to participate effectively in all decisions relating to its affairs. Indeed, it is capable of contributing to formulating proposals and solutions to the challenges facing the world as a whole. Morocco has translated this vision into practical and tangible royal initiatives. The most prominent of which are perhaps the royal initiative to enable Sahel states to access the Atlantic Ocean, as well as the African Atlantic States process, the African Atlantic gas pipeline project, as well as investments in regional infrastructure, cooperation in the areas of food security, fertilizer production, and training programs for African executives This is in addition to partnerships in the areas of health, renewable energy, and water resource management. Madam President, with regard to the North African region, thanks to the momentum initiated by His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him, the question of the Moroccan Sahara reached a historic turning point with the adoption by the Security Council of Resolution 2797 last October. Since then, this regional dispute has embarked on an irreversible course, breaking with the past and looking to the future with a view to its final settlement. This track rests on principles and parameters that admit no interpretation, nor any reading between the lines or in the margins, as some are vainly attempting, deluding themselves in flagrant denial of reality and total disregard for established truth. These principles, as set forth in the Security Council resolution, are as follows: First, There is no solution outside the framework of the autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty. Second, there is no approach or mechanism other than the political negotiation process under the auspices of the United Nations and on a sole basis, namely the autonomy initiative presented by the Kingdom of Morocco. Third, There can be no discussion or dispute regarding the responsibilities and obligations of the four parties clearly identified by Security Council Resolution 2797. Fourth, there will be no maintaining of the status quo preferred by the other parties. The train of political solution has already departed. Fifth, there is no credibility for interlocutors who violate the ceasefire and refuse to respect Security Council resolutions. Sixth and last, there can be no tolerance for the continued holding of the population of the camps as hostages for half a century in flagrant violation of international law and international humanitarian law. Alongside with its firm commitment to the final settlement of this regional dispute, affected regional dispute, the Kingdom of Morocco steadfastly continues to drive social and economic development in its southern provinces, particularly in areas of infrastructure, university education, health sector, and airports, among others. It is a fortunate coincidence that Tomorrow, God willing, the inhabitants of these Saharan provinces will fulfill their national and political duty by participating, as they have always done in the past, in the legislative elections of the Kingdom. In so doing, they will strengthen democratic representation and contribute to the day-to-day management of the needs of the inhabitants of the Moroccan provinces. Madam President, the Kingdom of Morocco, true to its constant approach, is determined to contribute effectively and responsibly to the maintenance of international peace and security. This is done in accordance with a realistic vision of international cooperation grounded in solidarity and with full respect for international law, national sovereignty, and territorial integrity. It is in this context that the Kingdom of Morocco has presented its candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for the term 2028-2029, so that it may continue to serve peace, collective security and multilateralism with full respect for the purposes and principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. It is the candidacy of a kingdom with a diplomatic heritage spanning several centuries, which carries the vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him, as an anchor for stability and sustainable development in the world. This candidacy also reflects the continued contribution of the Kingdom of Morocco to the three pillars of the United Nations, namely peace, development and the rule of law. I thank you.

I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Abroad of Morocco. We have heard the last speaker in the general debate for this meeting. We will continue the general debate tomorrow at 9:00 a.m. in this hall. The exercise of the right of reply has been requested. I propose that the time limits for statements in the exercise of the right of reply under this item be limited to five minutes for the first intervention and to three minutes for the second intervention. Is there any objection to this proposal? I hear none. It's so decided. Accordingly, pursuant to rule 72 of the rules of procedure of the Assembly, When a representative exceeds her or his allotted time, the President shall call on the speaker to order without delay, which will be done by means of automatic microphone cutoff. To assist delegations in managing their time, a countdown clock will be displayed on the screens. Members are also reminded that statements in the exercise of reply should be made by delegations from their seats. I call on the representative of Argentina.

In response to what was stated by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on the Malvinas Island, I wanted to remind you that the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding areas are part of the national territory of Argentina, illegally occupied by the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, are the subject of a sovereignty dispute between the two countries, recognized by the United Nations and by other international organizations. The illegal occupation by Britain of the islands is from January of 1833, when British forces occupied the islands, expelling the legitimate Argentinian authorities and substituting them this was at a time of peace and in violation of the international law valid at the time, was never recognized by Argentina. The General Assembly in its resolution 2065 recognizes the existence of a sovereignty dispute and urges the government of Argentina and the United Kingdom to renew negotiations in order to find a peaceful and lasting solution to the dispute as a way of decolonizing the territory. The special decolonization Committee has pronounced several times to this effect. The last time was in June of this year. Argentina reiterates its full readiness to resume bilateral negotiations, substantive ones, with the United Kingdom, in line with Resolution 2065. Our country reaffirms its commitment to a peaceful resolution of disputes through effective multilateralism and a rules-based order. We urge the United Kingdom to fulfill its obligations in the area of decolonization and to immediately cease its non-compliance with international law. In line with international law, the parties to a dispute must refrain from introducing unilateral modifications to a situation while the dispute is still pending resolution, nor adopt measures that aggravate the dispute. With regard to Malvinas, this refers to Resolution 39/49. which was adopted almost 50 years ago. In that resolution, the General Assembly urges the two parties to refrain from adopting decisions that imply introducing unilateral modifications in the situation while the islands go through a process recommended by the United Nations. The Republic of Argentina reaffirms its legitimate sovereignty right on the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia, and South Sandwich Islands, and the surrounding maritime areas, which are part and parcel of national Argentinian territory through its under law and based on history, Argentine Malvinas Argentine territory. Thank you.
